item.title: Chinese open-weight models lead, and distillation explains only one to two months of the gap
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-interconnects-中国开源权重模型领先-蒸馏只解释一两个月差距/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-interconnects-中国开源权重模型领先-蒸馏只解释一两个月差距/
item.description: Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation explains only one to two months of the gap; the real reasons are release cadence and task focus, and US companies are already building products on Chinese models.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation explains only one to two months of the gap; the real reasons are release cadence and task focus, and US companies are already building products on Chinese models.

This is a status briefing on open models written for Congress: dense with data, clear in its judgments, and suited to anyone who wants to grasp the US-China open-model landscape quickly.

0:00 Open weights is not the same thing as open source
An open-weight model releases only the weights and a license; an open-source model also releases the training code and data. America's genuinely open-source models are led by nonprofits, such as the Allen Institute for AI's Olmo, OpenAthena's Marin, and EleutherAI's Pythia. Nvidia's Nemotron is more open than most open-weight models, having released a large amount of training data, but because it has not released all of it, it still does not count as fully open source. The distinction matters: when people discuss "open source," what they are actually talking about is mostly open weights.

0:00 Chinese models have crossed the agentic capability threshold
GLM-5.2 and Kimi K3 delivered a step change in commercial viability, crossing an agentic capability threshold similar to the one Anthropic's Claude Code crossed in December 2025. Chinese open-weight models passed the US in these two key areas roughly 18 months ago. On Hugging Face downloads, China took the lead in July 2025, driven mainly by Alibaba's Qwen. Data from the ATOM project, which the author maintains, shows China's download lead has grown to about 1.6 billion out of a total of 3.2 billion, twice that of the US.

0:00 The benchmark score gap is stark
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, as of September 14, 2026, the top three are Chinese models: Z.ai's GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash score 45 and 42, and Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 scores 44. The US leaders are Thinking Machines' Inkling and Inkling Small, both scoring 26, and Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra at 23. The top US models were released in June and July 2026, and update less frequently than their Chinese counterparts. Chinese labs are closest on well-defined tasks like agentic coding, and lag further behind on open-ended scientific tasks such as physics and biology.

0:00 Distillation explains only one to two months of the gap
Distillation is a technique Chinese labs use commonly, training their own models on the outputs of stronger models, but the author estimates that even if distillation were blocked entirely, for instance by deploying KYC tools at Anthropic and OpenAI, the gap from the strongest US models to Chinese open-weight models would widen by only 1-2 months. Distillation matters most in new domains, and it cannot easily produce a comprehensively strong final model. Chinese labs release faster and with a narrower task distribution, which slightly inflates scores on public benchmarks, because all labs keep improving and later releases naturally score higher.

0:00 US companies are building products on Chinese models
Harvey, Cursor and DoorDash use Kimi, Airbnb uses Qwen, and Perplexity uses DeepSeek. A large number of young Silicon Valley startups use Chinese models to get a low-cost, flexible option. US startups sign enterprise agreements with Chinese model labs to license products for use, a new form of cross-border technology cooperation the author has not seen in his career. On OpenRouter, the Chinese model share has grown from about 70% to more than 80%, and weekly processed tokens have grown from about 1 trillion in September 2025 to about 80 trillion today. On OpenCode, Chinese models account for about 95% or more of inference volume.

0:00 Academia has already been taken over by Qwen
The author scanned papers in the five most popular ML categories on arXiv (cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.CV, cs.LG, stat.ML). In January 2023, papers mentioning any open model were 2%; by September 2026 they reached 50%. In April-May 2023, of about 12,000 new papers, 2,600 mentioned at least one open-model family, 5.5% mentioned Llama and 1% mentioned Chinese models. At Llama's peak in the fall of 2024, 23% mentioned Llama and 7.5% mentioned Qwen. Today Llama is still mentioned by about 21% of papers, while Qwen has risen to 30%. Any Chinese open-weight model is mentioned by more than 40% of papers, versus 30% for the US.

0:00 US models see higher adoption at equal capability
Research shows that US models see disproportionately high adoption when capability and scale are comparable. OpenAI's gpt-oss, its first open-weight models after ChatGPT, became one of the most widely adopted open-weight models ever. Google's Gemma 4 is one of the few models whose adoption approaches Qwen's most popular small models. Nvidia's Nemotron, despite being more capable at the same scale, has seen only middling adoption. This shows US models have brand and ecosystem advantages, but not enough to reverse the overall trend.

0:00 Open-model risk requires ecosystem-level preparation
The structural challenge of open-weight models is that there is almost no effective way to stop pieces of open-source software from falling into the wrong hands. If access to China's strongest open-weight models were restricted because of risk, the ones hurt would be US companies. HuggingFace once used a Chinese open-weight model to understand a cyberattack, because closed models refused the request. Managing open-weight model risk often comes down to ecosystem preparation. Open models are becoming an essential tool for AI diffusion, and continuing to invest in US open models is the best path to staying ahead of these risks.

item.title: A Glass of Water Has No Final Truth: Quantum Mechanics Forces Us to Give Up the Single Perspective
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-startweek-一杯水没有终极真相-量子力学逼我们放弃单一视角/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-startweek-一杯水没有终极真相-量子力学逼我们放弃单一视角/
item.description: Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not a new particle, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is many perspectives that enrich one another but do not converge.
item.content:encoded:
Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not a new particle, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is many perspectives that enrich one another but do not converge.

A four-person roundtable crossing physics, poetry, drama and economics; high density of quotable lines but the argument is loose. Worth listening if you want a few perspectives that can change your judgment; skip it if you want hard information.

2:06 A glass of water has no final version
Rovelli opens with a glass of water that the BBC provided: you look from one side, I look from the other, you wear glasses, I see a different colour. This glass of water can be a physical object (mass, velocity, position), it can be temperature and pressure, it can be the chemistry of H2O plus floating bits, it can be the global economy of being bottled in Italy and shipped to England, or it can simply be ‘we want to drink it’. His claim is: all these perspectives are real, none exhausts another, none contradicts another, and there is no ‘final glass of water’. This is anti-Platonic — he does not accept a distinction between a ‘level of appearances’ and a ‘fundamental level’.

6:13 We still have not digested quantum mechanics
Rovelli says what he is describing is not borrowed from philosophy but grown from inside physics. Physicists ran into quantum phenomena; quantum mechanics is a huge revolution, but ‘we have not yet digested quantum mechanics’ — the newspaper stories about experiments that ‘confirmed what I learned in a textbook in the 1970s’ show precisely that we still do not truly believe it. Take quantum mechanics seriously and what it says is this: the Enlightenment dream of ‘describing reality completely, determinately, clearly, independently of the observer’ does not hold. The observer here need not be a human; anything that interacts with something counts.

8:19 The deepest level of reality is not more objective
Rovelli turns it around: the most basic level of reality physics can reach is in fact not essentially different from the reality Lavinia deals with in poetry, or the characters in James's play deal with in economics — both are realities that allow different views, not a reality that is ‘absolutely objective underneath’. So quantum physics is not that hard; it simply has not been digested. The concrete physics is of course very complex, but poetry is complex and economics is complex too.

10:25 Scientists have always used metaphors
Rovelli says the words Lavinia uses could be lifted line by line into his book. What is an electron? ‘It is a grain, a grain of sand, but it is not really a grain of sand.’ Why is an electric field called a field? Because it is ‘a bit like a field in the countryside’. We think through metaphor, by taking old concepts apart and putting a piece of each together into a new concept. The goal is not to arrive at a final, perfect description of reality — a century ago we thought we could, but it does not work — but to gain a better understanding, a better way of navigating reality. He adds a crucial qualification: admitting that everything has a perspective does not mean all perspectives are equivalent, nor that there is no better and worse; it is only that the hope of ‘arriving at the final correct story about reality’ is empty — not unreachable, but meaningless.

12:27 Seeking the ultimate morality is itself wrong
Rovelli turns from ‘complexity’ to ‘value’: if you ask ‘what is the ultimate definition of good and evil, what is universal ethics’, he thinks this is itself a morally and ethically wrong approach. Our morals and values are powerful, important and indispensable not because they are outside us, but because they are inside us, and therefore equally perspectival. This section connects directly to James Graham's play — whose first line is ‘what is the good life’.

15:30 Do not be afraid to learn a jargon
Lavinia Greenlaw argues for embracing jargon: not everyone has to learn it, but if you are genuinely interested in something, do not be afraid to learn its language — a mechanic has to learn the names of parts, a surgeon has to learn the names of parts, a poet has to learn too. It lets you see more clearly, and it lets you see where something has gone wrong. She admits jargon can be exclusionary, but ‘that depends on the context in which you use it’, and ‘you can perform difficulty, poets and poems are probably very good at that, but that is not what difficulty means’. She gives the example of poems on the Underground: before everyone was on their phones, people would read a poem first and only then realise it was a poem, and that kind of engagement was far more direct and confident than sitting down and being told ‘now you are going to read a poem’.

22:55 Friction is treated as a problem to be solved
James Graham says modern culture fetishises ‘efficiency’ and strips out every layer of difficulty as friction. He gives a concrete image: emailing himself a script to save it, and a prompt pops up — ‘this is a long document, shall I summarise it for you?’ — and his reaction is ‘how rude, I want you to sit inside it and read it’. He connects this back to Bloomsbury and Keynes: meaning is discovered precisely in the friction, in the difficulty, in the process. He also says the collapse of reading is despairing, because reading demands personal investment, and today that investment is treated as a problem to be solved rather than something to be celebrated.

26:05 War refuses to acknowledge complexity
Rovelli uses International Peace Day on 21 September, and the words of the UN Secretary-General and the Pope, to connect the perspectival argument to war: war is to a large extent driven by greed and power games, but it always wraps itself in a hypocritical narrative — there is only one truth, only one good, we are the good ones, they are the bad ones, we tell the truth, they tell lies and propaganda. So war is built on a total refusal to be prepared to accept complexity, perspectives, and worldviews different from our own. The host Adam Rutherford immediately offers a counterexample: we also always need to seek simplicity, and if you embraced difficulty and acted scholarly all day you might get nothing done and enjoy nothing. Lavinia's response pulls the topic back to rhetoric: language therefore matters more than ever, and poetry and poetics can teach people how to argue.

item.title: Apple has no frontier model of its own, but wants to win again with a foldable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果没有自己的前沿模型-却想靠折叠屏再赢一次/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果没有自己的前沿模型-却想靠折叠屏再赢一次/
item.description: Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the entire event had not a single new AI feature; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet is on the foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.
item.content:encoded:
Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the entire event had not a single new AI feature; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet is on the foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.

Mark Gurman is the most accurate reporter on Apple, and this episode strings together the executive reshuffle, the AI roadmap, the privacy controversy and the foldable prediction into one line, with high information density.

5:09 The biggest difference between Ternus and Cook is that he'll make the call
Gurman says the event was almost interchangeable with the Cook era, with the only difference being that Ternus opened by offering a view on AI. The mechanism he gives is management style: you bring an idea to Cook and he keeps probing with questions, in many cases not making a single decision, it's collective decision-making; you go to Ternus and he gives you a decision, gives you an opinion, you may hate the opinion, but he has a position. Gurman stresses this is exactly the biggest difference between the two men from talking to insiders, and it explains why Ternus talked about AI first thing on stage.

8:20 The 2026 event had not a single new AI feature
Gurman points out that Apple held a big product event in September 2026 yet launched no notable new AI features, and the roughly 15-minute opening just retold the Apple Intelligence story of the past two years. His explanation: Apple has gone as far on AI as it can and can only tell the best story with the cards it holds; and Apple has no AI-centric device, so it has to prop up the iPhone as its AI device until a killer device appears and it can change the narrative.

13:29 Under Cook, Apple became an institution
Gurman distinguishes the Cook era from the Jobs era: in the Cook era people's relationship with Apple is a relationship with an institution, one that spans the globe and is enormous, like IBM; the Jobs era was one new product after another redefining categories. He also corrects the host's judgment on Vision Pro — every time he writes that Vision Pro is on life support, he gets dozens of reactions close to death-threat level, because some people have built businesses around spatial computing and some consumers paid four thousand dollars for it.

20:45 Apple spent five years swapping out the old guard one by one
Gurman reconstructs the rhythm of this handover: in 2023 Cook began saying at every executive meeting that succession had to be taken seriously; at the time the top brass either had five hundred million in the bank or were billionaires, and were close in age. So they lined up an order and went one by one — at the end of 2024 CFO Luca Maestri retired, replaced by Kevin Parekh; in 2025 COO Jeff Williams retired, succeeded by his deputy; in 2026 the general counsel changed, with Jennifer Newstead poached from Meta; and only at the end of 2026 did Cook hand over to Ternus. Gurman calls this retention strategy Hotel California: you never want to leave.

28:07 The chip chief was kept with a made-up title
Gurman says the second most important person at Apple now is the hardware head, who built Apple Silicon, Apple's key differentiator. In late summer or early autumn last year, he went to tell Cook he was quitting, right during the preparations for Ternus's succession. Cook got him to stay and take part in the transition, promising him the title of chief hardware officer, which Apple had never had, once Ternus took over, letting him keep his existing team and also take over Ternus's side of the business. Gurman judges this is not a long-term arrangement, and that the man already wants to leave again — he conquered the Mac, shed Intel and Qualcomm, and Apple has no next goal, so he may leave within a year or two, at which point the hardware engineering team will have to be split up again, because no successor carries his industry weight.

33:15 Willing to spend tens of billions on modems, yet says it needn't own AI
What Gurman finds most absurd is executives saying in interviews over the past year that ‘we never owned search, we don't need to own AI’. He counters: these are two completely different things, and Apple spent tens of billions to own a cellular modem that had already been commoditized, acquiring and fixing Intel's modem business — willing to do that for a modem but unwilling to own AI is ridiculous. The internal idea was originally to partner with Google as a stopgap until it could build its own models, but Gurman says he has seen no evidence that Apple is restarting its own model effort, making big AI acquisitions, or paying AI researchers high salaries.

48:53 All-day watch transcription stepped on the privacy landmine
Gurman's reaction to the Apple Watch's all-day listening feature was ‘I can't believe they did it’. The feature only transcribes, doesn't record or store, and a double tap shows you the last 15 seconds of what someone said to you, without their consent. He says Apple knows the next-generation interface needs a degree of always-on capture, but the societal privacy problem is unsolved: technical white papers, private cloud compute and encryption can't hold back the social backlash. He thinks Apple could have put audio and visual intelligence together next year and told a coherent privacy story, but as it stands it's boiling the frog slowly.

57:05 Foldables will become the new normal within a decade
Gurman offers a bold prediction: foldables will become the new normal within a decade. He draws an analogy with smartphone penetration — at the end of 2006 smartphones were about 6% of the market, now 85%, and within five or six years they were past half; the iPhone itself wasn't that source, but it pulled everyone into the smartphone game, and he thinks the iPhone Duo will do the same for the phone market. He also mentions the iPhone's number migration feature, hinting the future may be a combination of a foldable for work and a smaller, lighter phone for weekends with family.

item.title: America's Manufacturing Hollowing Isn't a Capability Problem, It's a Financial Return Problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.description: Chris Power says America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statements, while China manages it like national security; tariffs are just an imperfect corrective tool, and the core issue is to stop American consumers from subsidizing rivals' industrial capacity.
item.content:encoded:
Chris Power says America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statements, while China manages it like national security; tariffs are just an imperfect corrective tool, and the core issue is to stop American consumers from subsidizing rivals' industrial capacity.

Two frontline hardware founders explain the real bottlenecks of American reindustrialization: not technology, but trust, cost, and supply chain definitions. High information density, with the most valuable part being the breakdown of tariffs and subsidies in the second half.

2:02 The reserve currency is the first step of decline
Chris Power gives a four-step cycle: great powers first have a generative population and the best industrial capacity, then win or prevent a war, then become extremely lazy, and finally outsource the things that made them successful. He says this cycle repeats roughly every 150 years: the Dutch gave way to the British, the British gave way to the Americans, and each time industrial power was re-traded for financial power, the world's reserve currency changed. This judgment was the starting point for him founding Hadrian: you think you're Mike Tyson at his peak, but your opponent thinks you're the Mike Tyson before Buster Douglas knocked him out.

9:10 90% of the factory is a software problem
Chris Power says the biggest misconception about advanced manufacturing is that seeing people moving things in a factory means it's a humanoid robot problem. In reality, 90% of advanced manufacturing is smart people sitting at computers doing digital engineering, or operating a very dumb computer on the shop floor. Welders or machinists have to stand in front of the machine because the system isn't closed-loop; they do trigonometry in their heads to judge whether the tool is about to break. So Hadrian positions itself as a software company, doing the work of breaking physical tasks into high-judgment setups, then handing them off to robots, CNC, or welding systems for execution.

14:14 Software is done in Silicon Valley, hardware in LA
Tom Mueller says the aerospace talent ecosystem in Southern California is recovering; three or four years after SpaceX was founded in 2002, the aerospace employment curve in the South Bay started to rise. He lists what this area is simultaneously doing: nuclear energy companies, drone companies, defense companies, 3D printing companies, and Anduril in Orange County. The two companies poach from each other and compete for talent, and Northrop Grumman is right across the street from Impulse. Tom's summary: software is done in Silicon Valley, hardware in LA.

15:17 Vertical integration is to learn the problem, not to save money
Tom Mueller explains the real logic of SpaceX-style vertical integration: the first development engine or spacecraft must be built in-house, because you need to learn all the assembly and machining problems during the prototype phase. If you hand it to a machine shop from the start, and the drawings have problems or the parts don't fit when made, you learn nothing. Once the design converges, then outsource. Chris Power adds that every company should keep 10% to 15% of in-house capacity, because there's always a "hot pot" moment when you need a genius to make something in an hour to meet a flight milestone, but scale must happen externally.

16:18 Outsourcing decisions are about trust, not finance
Chris Power says what's bought and sold in manufacturing is trust. Hadrian's vertical integration strategy is to outsource as much as possible to every reindustrialization startup and small business, because there are too many projects to run. But they will vertically integrate the links where they "don't believe you can deliver on time." This isn't a financial trade-off; they'd rather spend an extra two million dollars on equipment and hire a team than bet the risk on a traditional foundry that has been late on every submarine project for the past thirty years. His exact words: most of America is incompetent when it comes to trust and scheduling.

19:20 In WWII, America was China
Chris Power uses WWII as an analogy: German engineers crushed America in engineering, but America wore them down with McDonald's-style mass production and better logistics. He says America played the role in WWII that China plays today—not by having the best engineering, but by producing the most. Now the situation is reversed: US missile stockpiles run out in seven days in war games, China built 2,600 ships while America built six. His conclusion: you can have the best Raytheon missiles, but if you can't mass-produce them, you have no options.

21:23 The robot bottleneck is the speed of training data
Chris Power says the robot competition ultimately depends on software, and software, especially AI, now depends on the velocity of training data, which in turn depends on physical-world deployment—that is, mass manufacturing. So this isn't a friendly competition between American companies over "whether Tesla sells more Optimus or Google wins"; it's a civilization-level confrontation. Tom Mueller adds from the space perspective: building on the Moon and Mars requires robot legions rather than humans, because the environment is too dangerous and too expensive; good robots need three things—dexterous hands, vision which is basically solved, and an AI brain.

29:40 Tariffs are an imperfect corrective tool
Chris Power says manufacturing has four inputs: energy, labor, cost of capital, and export tariffs. He has done the math: even if Hadrian's labor and energy costs were both zero, importing components from China would still be three times cheaper than buying raw materials in America and making them yourself. He believes China has operated industrial policy as national security since 1985, subsidizing energy, labor, capital, and export tariffs, while America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statement returns. The problem with tariffs is enforcement: banning only China and not Singapore means Chinese companies route through Singapore; differences in definitions of raw materials and assembly also inadvertently hurt American companies importing components from Mexico.

item.title: He Cooked the Chickpea Pasta Into Mush, Then Survived by Telling People to Brew It Like Tea
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-howibuilt-把鹰嘴豆意面煮成糊后-他靠-像泡茶一样泡-活了下来/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-howibuilt-把鹰嘴豆意面煮成糊后-他靠-像泡茶一样泡-活了下来/
item.description: Banza's first scaled-up production run failed across the board: 20,000 boxes of pasta fell apart the moment they hit boiling water. They didn't destroy them. They slapped on a sticker saying "brew it like tea" and shipped — because not shipping meant losing the retailer forever.
item.content:encoded:
Banza's first scaled-up production run failed across the board: 20,000 boxes of pasta fell apart the moment they hit boiling water. They didn't destroy them. They slapped on a sticker saying "brew it like tea" and shipped — because not shipping meant losing the retailer forever.

The founder's account is dense with failure detail: three scrapped production batches, a kidney stone, being thrown out of the factory, a 30% week-over-week decline. Worth hearing for anyone who wants to know how you survive a near-death moment.

5:14 The starting point wasn't a business insight, it was a runny nose
In college Brian's fridge held nothing but hummus, eating was just "fuel" to him, and he cycled between antibiotics and steroids for so long he was nearly facing surgery. It was his father, an orthodontist, who got him to try an elimination diet, and that's how he found that wheat-based foods triggered sinus inflammation — one beer and the next day he couldn't breathe. The ENT told him: I don't know what you're talking about, but if it works, keep doing it. That private problem later became the product definition: high-protein, high-fiber, gluten-free pasta, doing what Chobani did for yogurt.

10:26 The first recipe had chia in it and was too sticky to look at
He bought Bob's Red Mill chickpea flour on Amazon and followed blogs for combinations. Version one was chickpeas plus eggs plus chia — the chia made it so sticky the result was ugly. With no rolling pin he used a wine bottle; with no pasta cutter he used a knife, dusting flour on the table as he cut to keep it from sticking. Version two dropped the chia, leaving just chickpeas and eggs, and was clearly better, but to make it usable for more people he added tapioca starch and xanthan gum back in and committed to a vegan route. His first capital expenditure was an Atlas Mercado hand-crank pasta machine, about $30 on Amazon. He got up at 5 a.m. every day to make pasta, put on country music, and his roommates thought he was insane.

20:49 Going from 200 pounds an hour to 1,000 scaled the mistakes too
They first found a tiny gluten-free factory in Michigan that could only do 150 to 200 pounds an hour — wildly inefficient, but they could learn while running. To get into 190 Meijer stores and 2 Eataly locations, that capacity wasn't enough, so they found what was then the largest gluten-free pasta factory in the country, outside Los Angeles. The problem: that plant had only ever run rice and corn pasta, never legumes. Scaled up to roughly 1,000 pounds an hour, the pasta coming out looked fine and turned into total mush the moment it was boiled. Each trial run was 8,000 to 10,000 pounds, and a failure meant the die costs and ingredient costs were all gone, while they had only a little over $100,000 on hand.

26:02 He got thrown out of the factory for asking the operator
After several failed trial runs, Brian ignored the other side's objections and went straight to the line operator to ask what was actually going wrong. The worker said "this corn smells weird," and he answered: that's not corn, we're not making corn pasta today, it's chickpeas. He realized on the spot that communication had broken down completely, and right after that he was escorted out of the plant. At the same time the distributor was threatening him: if you don't fulfill this purchase order, you will never work with this retailer again. He later estimated this shipment would cost nearly every dollar they had.

28:07 The fix was don't boil it — brew it like tea
With nowhere left to turn they started testing: boil one minute, two minutes, three minutes, then stop boiling altogether — bring water to a boil, turn off the heat, and let the pasta steep in the hot water. What came out of steeping was better than what came out of boiling, or at least it didn't fall apart. Brian says he wasn't proud of the product, and it bothered him to sell it under his own brand, but he knew it was life or death. The packaging was already printed, so they could only make extra stickers reading "Banza is easier to cook than regular pasta — brew it like tea," and then find people to hand-apply them to 20,000 boxes. Once that shipment went out, they immediately pulled out of the big factory and went back to the small one in Michigan.

35:18 The box is orange because every other pasta box is blue
They noticed that nearly every pasta package on the shelf at the time was blue — Brian put it as "you'd think they'd colluded." Orange contrasts most strongly with blue, and orange was also the color he'd loved since watching Nickelodeon as a kid, so it became the brand color. They made trade-offs on the packaging copy too: putting "chickpeas" in the most prominent spot would scare off a lot of people, and so would gluten-free, so the gluten-free certification went on the side while the front led with high protein and high fiber — making consumers feel this was "a product for me," not "a product that isn't for me."

41:31 The glyphosate report cut weekly sales by a third
Moms Across America published a report claiming glyphosate residue was detected in Banza products. Brian saw the Google alert during a one-on-one meeting; he says his heart sank and his mind jumped twenty steps ahead. He wanted to verify first, so he put out only a statement saying "we are investigating" — which was nowhere near enough for the most panicked people. The lab results were delayed again and again, dragging on for three weeks. The final published result was 98% below the allegation, but not zero — still a very low level, and below the EWG's risk benchmark. He decided to make the supply chain 100% traceable and to join the Detox Project's certification program.

52:15 Natural channel recovery was far slower than ordinary channels
The sales recovery was a mixed bag: some channels came back better than before, but the natural channel recovered far more slowly — and that was exactly the customer base with the best repeat purchase and the highest sales per store. Brian says this actually makes sense, because natural channel consumers are the most susceptible to this kind of information. What he does now: he keeps alerts on for anywhere Banza and glyphosate are mentioned, and personally goes on Reddit to reply and add context, with the goal of making it impossible for the story to be seen without its context. He also admits he should have acknowledged what was happening faster and more visibly at the time.

item.title: AI Won't Replace People — What Replaces Them Is Work Nobody Wrote Down
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-twentyvc-ai-不会取代人-取代人的是没被写下来的工作/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-twentyvc-ai-不会取代人-取代人的是没被写下来的工作/
item.description: Models are interchangeable; what's actually valuable is the manual a company writes of how work gets done — that "map of work" is the irreplaceable asset of the AI era, and the only precondition for a company to train its own model.
item.content:encoded:
Models are interchangeable; what's actually valuable is the manual a company writes of how work gets done — that "map of work" is the irreplaceable asset of the AI era, and the only precondition for a company to train its own model.

Daniel Dines breaks down the real bottleneck of AI landing inside enterprises from UiPath's front-line view, with a high density of counter-consensus claims — suited to anyone trying to judge the pace of enterprise AI adoption.

6:17 AI does not change its own weights on the job
Daniel argues the biggest difference between AI and humans is not reasoning ability, but that AI does not change its own weights on the job. A human is changed by a job; AI just writes things into a notepad. He gives the example of two chefs: one who has cooked Japanese cuisine for 20 years, one who has cooked Italian for 20 years — give them the same recipe and what they produce is completely different. This is not something you can replicate by writing the company down on paper, because human judgment comes from years of being reshaped by the work. So on the claim that "there are millions of Einsteins in the data center," Daniel thinks what Dario meant is that there are millions of entities with partial reasoning ability — not Einsteins who can learn on the job the way a person does.

16:29 Probabilistic tech shouldn't do work that demands precision
Daniel raises another limit on AI: precision. Every step AI takes is probabilistic — even if each step is 99% correct, after 100 steps the overall success rate may be only 60%. So make AI do long multiplication over and over and it will eventually get it wrong. His conclusion: just because a tool can do something doesn't mean you should use it for that thing. ChatGPT looks like it's doing arithmetic, but behind the scenes it's calling a computer tool — the precision is not provided by ChatGPT. Extend that logic to the enterprise level: all work that demands precision should run on precise technology; there is no reason for it to run on probabilistic technology.

18:34 Deploying AI hasn't gotten easier; deploying automation has
Daniel points to an asymmetry inside enterprises: deploying AI agents is no easier than it was two years ago, but deploying automation has become much easier, because you can use coding agents to generate the automation. He lists ChatGPT, chain of thoughts and coding agents as the three main milestones. Coding agents work at "design time": people use them to build automations that run precisely every time at "execution time"; and when an automation breaks because an upstream system changed, AI can come back and fix it. The result is that AI is generating the software that runs the company, and that software cannot change its behaviour in real time — it can be audited, tested and read by people. This is the pattern he sees taking shape in enterprises right now.

23:46 Blind layoffs cut the people AI most needs
In his book Daniel introduces the concept of the "credentialed middle": companies used to hire people on the basis of deep domain credentials in some field, and that is exactly the kind of expertise AI helps with most. His judgment is counter-intuitive — you will be inclined to cut the people who are not the biggest experts in the domain, but those are precisely the people you will need to supplement expert work with AI. He gives the example of a law firm: it used to hire 25 interns a year, this year it hired only 4. He agrees most roles will need fewer people, but the key question is "which people." His criterion: keep the people with the most initiative, who can maintain client relationships, who can mentor newcomers, who carry the company culture — because AI cannot show initiative in the human sense.

25:51 What decides whether AI can take over is how clear the framework is
Harry argues that work like finance and accounting is highly verifiable, so it is easy for AI to replace. Daniel disagrees outright: it is not a question of verifiability, but of whether the job is framed by a framework someone else has already defined. He says finance is precisely an area where the framework is unclear — receive an invoice or an order and there can be different ways to handle it; for instance, whether Nvidia would ship to OpenAI first is a rule that may never have been written down. If the rule isn't captured by a framework, AI can't learn it. So a company must first hand AI the "map of work": all workflows, all exceptions, all processes, all systems. This is also what he keeps stressing: models are interchangeable; the map of work and the processes around it are where the real value lies.

29:01 Use agents to interview employees and draw work as a map
UiPath has launched a technology called cartography, as a discipline that helps companies surface how work actually gets done. Concretely, it uses a product called a cartographer agent to interview real business experts and have them record what they are doing, with the agent following up in real time: why did you change how you handled this invoice because the postcode was different? Why did you choose another path? That is how exceptions get dug out one by one. Then it aggregates data from multiple people to generate a real-time process map. With that "map of work" in hand, you use coding agents to design how the process should be transformed, and ultimately, through "printing software," push the process from purely manual point A toward a state where fewer people operate systems and more automation and agentic AI do.

34:15 Vibe coding is easy for prototypes, hard for production
Daniel admits UiPath tried vibe coding; at first it looked astonishing, but pushing it into production hit a wall: connectors, permissions, auditing, security — all of it has to be maintained. He gives his own example of writing a procurement tool: initially it was written entirely by AI, but the database schema was completely wrong and someone had to rebuild the structure. His conclusion is that going from prototype to production is where the real work is, not writing the code itself. In the end you will very likely pay as much as, or more than, the tool you replaced — while also consuming the bandwidth of your best people. So he does not think systems of record like Salesforce will be replaced by vibe coding.

45:34 The legal AI opportunity is in process, not model calls
Harry runs the numbers: the US legal industry is a $300 billion market, and if 30% of the labour can be replaced that is $90 billion in revenue. Daniel counters that the $90 billion will not convert into token revenue — maybe only 10%, so a $10 billion token opportunity. His judgment: for legal opinions, open-source models and frontier models are both good enough; what is actually valuable is the custom workflows built around legal processes. If Harvey and Lagora just call a model once for you to get a legal opinion, that is not a hundred-billion-dollar market; but if they really draw the work as a map, build the workflows, and create a legal department for you, the value is far greater.

item.title: Even Legal-Cannabis States Can't Escape: A Federal Ban Is About to Empty the THC Shelves
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-indicator-大麻合法州也躲不过-联邦禁令要清空-thc-货架/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-indicator-大麻合法州也躲不过-联邦禁令要清空-thc-货架/
item.description: A loophole in the 2018 farm bill let hemp-derived THC grow into a $28 billion industry. Now Congress wants to close it — and even states where cannabis is legal will feel it, because they'll lose the cheap alternative.
item.content:encoded:
A loophole in the 2018 farm bill let hemp-derived THC grow into a $28 billion industry. Now Congress wants to close it — and even states where cannabis is legal will feel it, because they'll lose the cheap alternative.

Eight minutes on how a regulatory loophole grew into an industry and how it gets cut off in one stroke — for anyone watching policy risk and regulatory arbitrage.

0:00 Legal-cannabis states don't escape a federal ban
Half of US states have legal recreational cannabis, but the reason THC drinks, vapes and gummies can be sold openly in states that ban cannabis is a loophole left by the 2018 farm bill: it allows low-concentration THC from hemp. After lab processing, that low concentration is enough to mimic a cannabis high, which is how you get Delta 8, Delta 9 — and, as the show jokes, by now Delta 11. Congress now wants to close the loophole, and it's using a stricter ban to do it. The key point is that this is a federal ban, so even if your state has legal cannabis, you get hit.

1:00 What's being banned is a $28 billion industry
The show puts the size at $28 billion and says the industry could disappear before the end of this year. Tennessee has already gone first: since July it has banned most THC hemp products, and a local reporter described herself as already living in a "post-hemp world." State legislators even beat Congress to it, banning full-spectrum CBD and smokable flower first. For retailers, farmers and processors, this isn't a policy debate — it's a choice that has to be made before year-end.

3:07 Farmers are going back from hemp to blackberries and corn
Tennessee farmer Lee Crabtree's farm used to grow mostly CBD-variety hemp. The new state law makes selling those products illegal, so he's gone back to traditional seasonal crops like blackberries and corn. The family still has the industrial kitchen from its CBD food days; his wife Stacy now uses that big stainless-steel counter to cut grapes for chicken salad and sells it at a roadside farmers market. Lee says income is down, and if the traditional crops don't sell, he'll have to go find a job. This is what the ban looks like landing on one household.

5:08 The regulator's case: consumers don't know what they're drinking
Tennessee Republican Representative William Lamberth uses a drinks analogy: someone buying Sprite expects Sprite, not beer; someone buying beer expects beer, not tequila; someone buying tequila expects not to get Sprite. He says the goal is for consumers to know exactly what they're buying. But farmers, even when they agree with the logic, worry the law goes too far. The show gives the other side too: big companies are laying people off, and some are simply moving across state lines — Emily Schaeferich's company Burning Acre moved from Columbia, Tennessee, to North Carolina to keep growing, and she admits ripping up an entire retail, manufacturing and wholesale supply chain "definitely costs a lot of money."

6:10 Moving to another state may be wasted effort
Hemp economist Beau Whitney calls the nationwide ban taking effect in December an "extinction-level event." His mechanism: cannabis can only be grown in certain states, while hemp can be grown and shipped anywhere, so hemp businesses can build massive-scale capacity, push costs down and ship nationwide; cannabis, by contrast, needs a separate supply chain per state and can't get hemp's economies of scale. The result is that hemp-derived food is far cheaper than the cannabis equivalent. So even in states with legal recreational cannabis, consumers will feel the pinch when they lose the cheap alternative.

7:13 The ban also takes out state tax revenue
The show pulls out economies of scale on its own to explain: the more you produce of the same good, the lower the unit cost, and the savings can be passed to consumers. That's also why hemp-derived food is cheaper than cannabis products. But consumers aren't the only ones affected. For a lot of state budgets, losing the hemp industry means losing a sizable source of tax revenue — in Tennessee alone, a $54 million budget hole. Beau Whitney also says it could put hundreds of thousands of jobs at risk.

7:13 The delay just moves it from November to December
The White House has urged Congress to delay or amend the ban; the Senate currently supports it, and the House voted earlier this month to delay it too. But these moves only push the effective date from November to December — a one-month delay. For companies that have already moved across state lines and rebuilt supply chains, a month changes nothing — they may have just moved the whole business only to find the industry destroyed in December.

8:14 Those staying behind switch to fiber hemp
Tennessee farmer Bill Corbin, in Springfield, is preparing the first fiber hemp crop for the French company Hemp-It; this hemp goes into rope, packaging and auto parts. He says there isn't a person in the industry who didn't know this day was coming, that the industry was unsustainable to begin with, and he agrees with legislators' efforts to suppress recreational use of hemp derivatives. But he worries about medical consumers: he himself is older and has arthritis, relies heavily on full-spectrum CBD, and the products left after the ban may not be strong enough for older people or those trying to avoid opioid painkillers.

item.title: The Bat Doesn't Know What It's Like to Be a Bat Either
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-pel-蝙蝠自己也不知道当蝙蝠是什么感觉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-pel-蝙蝠自己也不知道当蝙蝠是什么感觉/
item.description: The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.
item.content:encoded:
The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.

The second half of episode 400, and listenable on its own. The first half is about theories of consciousness; the second half unexpectedly slides into animal ethics, and the four of them never do settle their disagreement.

1:07 A bat having an inner world is not the same as being conscious
Christopher summarises Dennett's response: he flatly denies Nagel — we can talk about what it's like to be a bat in all sorts of ways (by first ruling out the things bats don't do, for instance), and with enough information we eventually get there, because so-called "what it's like to be a bat" just is the discriminative, dispositional states the bat has. Dylan supplies the step Dennett actually rejects: drawing on von Uexküll's Umwelt and Innenwelt (surrounding world and inner world), Dennett grants that the bat has an inner world, which isn't crazy; what he won't accept is going straight from "has an inner world" to "therefore consciousness exists", and that latter step is exactly the one Nagel uses to prove consciousness exists. Our mode of access is heterophenomenology: treat the bat's behaviour and physiology as a text in need of interpretation.

5:37 Consciousness is not an all-or-nothing property
Christopher reads out a passage from Dennett: are language-less animals not conscious at all? Dennett says the question shouldn't be taken as a given challenge, because it presupposes "something we've had a hard time getting rid of" — that consciousness is an all-or-nothing property, splitting the universe into two utterly different categories: things that have it and things that don't. That binary is what Dennett wants to dismantle; what he wants is consciousness in degrees. Christopher then offers his own version: he doesn't want to accept property dualism, he wants to deny the hard problem, because subjectivity can perfectly well have a biological and evolutionary explanation — agency and subjectivity co-evolved; a physical process organised from the inside "feeling like something" is a real biological phenomenon.

12:57 The bat doesn't know what it's like to be a bat either
Seth pushes the argument to its extreme: it isn't "we don't know what it's like to be a bat", it's that there is no "what it's like to be a bat as seen from the bat's side" at all; the bat itself doesn't know either, because it lacks the machinery to string experiences into a narrative and give them names. Dylan immediately marks out the cost of this inference: if anything with dynamic activity has its own experience, then atoms count too, and that's panpsychism. Christopher says you don't have to go as far as atoms, but concedes that the direction really does sound like panpsychism — he'd rather use a threshold: you need a feedback loop of perception and action before you can talk about a new way of being.

14:35 Even plants have a perspective in some sense
Mark digs up a line from Dennett's book: the perspective of a conscious observer is a refined descendant of the first replicators' primitive perspective of "dividing the world into good and bad" — on that account even plants have a perspective in this sense, and "perspective" thereby becomes a metaphor. Christopher then offers gradualism: from sponges to mantis shrimp to humans, subjectivity accumulates layer by layer and gets thicker and thicker, with a fuzzy threshold in between. Dylan wants to nail the threshold down harder: you can't use "complex" as the criterion, since weather is a complex self-maintaining system too; the difference is that living things can replicate themselves and have a wholeness, so the only thing the Earth lacks is its own replication.

19:47 You are a bunch of things, not a soul
Mark finds Dennett's 1994 reply collection Get Real, which uses snakes as an example: a snake has no central representation of "mouse", it just responds to prey through three separate sensory systems. Dennett's point is that the perceptual system we take to be a single whole is really a pile of little homunculi each making its own discriminations; you are not an Aristotelian form, a soul, an organisation that runs you — we are all a bunch of things. Christopher objects: failure to integrate information processing doesn't mean there's no self — the two hemispheres of a split-brain patient are also separate, and we don't conclude from that that he has no self; the snake may still have a more ancient, minimal sense of boundary and evaluative experience.

27:39 Reducing experience to discrimination looks a lot like behaviourism
Christopher says he agrees with Dennett 99%, and is stuck on the 1%: when Dennett wants to reduce a person to dispositional states, saying that experiencing red is nothing over and above being able to discriminate red from non-red and being in that discriminative state, it sounds like behaviourism. Seth offers a defence: even if the substrate is just discriminative states, subjective experience, the self, is a composite stitched together out of memory, imagination, representation and symbolic language — it weaves scattered discriminative states into a story with descriptions, meanings and colour, and that story is me. Christopher agrees about the narrative self, but points out that the bat lacks the metacognitive capacity to construct that kind of self.

38:54 You can club an iguana, but not a rabbit
Mark says "everyone is a world" is a good moral fiction, but he doesn't know how to apply it to animals: Florida has too many iguanas, and he encourages everyone to go out and club them — he says that's completely fine and humane; swap in a rabbit and he won't accept it. Seth offers an evolutionary explanation: our feelings about animals domesticated over tens of thousands of years, wild animals and reptiles were never the same to begin with, and this doesn't conflict with "the self is a narrative centre of gravity". Christopher anchors it in valence: animals are not reflex machines, they are situated perspectives that evaluate, and that is the reason they enter moral consideration — he says that after reading Lars Chittka's The Mind of a Bee, the way he deals with bees changed.

46:10 Take away caring and nothing is left of pain
Mark turns to where Dennett talks specifically about pain: what is the functional relation of pain? If you take away "caring about it, wanting to get away from it", take away everything else, and leave only the sensation of pain, then nothing is left — your not liking the pain is itself part of the pain. Mark says this is exactly Dennett's attitude to philosophical zombies: imagine a person identical to you in biological makeup, reactions, even internal relations, but the light of consciousness never came on — Dennett thinks this is so absurd that it's hard even to explain to scientists.

item.title: Germany's CDU Falls Out of a State Parliament: The Era of the Centre Is Over
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.description: The CDU won under 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz's authority is gone, and the populist far left and far right hold an overwhelming majority among voters under 35.
item.content:encoded:
The CDU won under 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz's authority is gone, and the populist far left and far right hold an overwhelming majority among voters under 35.

This is a piece of German domestic political commentary, not an interview. Information density is moderate, but it lays out the judgment that "populism has become the mainstream" very clearly — suited to anyone watching the direction of European politics.

0:00 The CDU is shut out of a state parliament for the first time
In the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state election, the CDU won under 5% of the vote and therefore holds no seats in that state parliament — the first time this has happened in the history of the Federal Republic. In the same election the AfD took about 38% of the vote, once again becoming the state's largest party. The author calls this the "final nail in the coffin" for Merz: he may hang on as chancellor for a few more weeks or months, but his authority has vanished and his capacity to shape the country is completely exhausted — in political language, "a dead man walking."

0:00 The CDU's decline came later than the SPD's but is just as fatal
The CDU is the most important party in postwar German history, governing the Federal Republic for 53 of the past 77 years; from Adenauer and Kohl to Merkel, it left its mark on every aspect of the country. The author notes that in the early 2000s everyone was talking about "the crisis of social democracy," and the SPD fell from over 40% support to record lows; in hindsight, the fate of the centre-left big tent was merely a leading indicator of a broader crisis of the entire political centre, and the CDU then walked the same road. The era of what Germans call the Volksparteien — catch-all parties capable of mobilising most of the vote — has effectively ended.

0:00 Populists are not a fringe phenomenon but the most important political force
The author says this has been the most-asked question of the past decade: "Will the populist wave last, or is it about to peak?" In the summer of 2016, when Trump became the Republican nominee and Britain voted for Brexit, the answer seemed obvious to him; now the answer is undeniable — the populists are here to stay. What looked abnormal a few years ago has, whether you like it or not, become the mainstream. Populist politicians now hold power in the United States, India, Turkey and many parts of the democratic world, and have a very high probability of taking office in France and Brazil in the coming months. Even where they remain in opposition, they are already strong enough to destroy any sense of business as usual.

0:00 The rise of one extremist party is feeding another
In the Berlin state election, Die Linke took 26% of the vote and emerged the big winner. The party descends from the SED, which ruled East Germany with an iron fist; after reunification it initially appealed mainly to older voters nostalgic for the security of the communist system, and in recent years it has reinvented itself in the image of the global illiberal left — the author considers it roughly comparable to Zack Polanski's Greens in Britain or the more extreme parts of the DSA in the United States. During the campaign, some of its supporters were filmed chanting "Yalla, Yalla Intifada!"; on election night, the head of a notorious crime family visited the party's election party and cheerfully told the media he felt an affinity with it. The party's leader will very likely now become the next mayor of Berlin — the first time an heir to the SED takes power in the capital.

0:00 Voters under 35 have swung to the two extremes
Another notable feature of the two elections is the age distribution. The SPD and CDU, which once dominated Germany's political landscape, draw most of their support from pensioners. Among voters under 35, Die Linke and the AfD hold unassailable majorities in both Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. From this the author concludes that an even larger shift toward the extremes will come in the next few years. This also explains why the collapse of the centre is not a one-off election accident: the structure of the electorate itself is tipping the scales toward the two ends.

0:00 Mecklenburg-Vorpommern's left coalition is just an election accident
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, because a batch of other parties all failed to clear the 5% threshold for entering parliament, a broad left coalition just barely won enough votes to govern. But the author stresses that this is an election accident unlikely to repeat — a gap of a few thousand votes would leave the state completely ungovernable. This point is crucial: when centrist parties fall below the threshold, they do not merely lose their own seats; they push the governability of the entire state to the edge of a cliff.

0:00 Do not surrender, and do not deny that the problem is real
The author explicitly rejects two responses. The first is to urge the centre to surrender: if the political centre cannot hold, moderates might as well defect to the extremists "on their own side." He thinks this is wrong — neither Die Linke nor the AfD can solve the real problems Germany faces, and despite their enormous differences, the two have conspicuous similarities, from their ambiguity toward Moscow to their persistent inability to purge antisemites from their own ranks. The second is to keep denying reality: for a decade the centre has attributed the extremists' success to foreign interference, social media algorithms, some candidate's tactical blunder, or the stupidity, sexism or racism of voters. The author says these ways of blinding oneself to the facts in front of you may be comforting, but they are equally dangerous.

item.title: Going overseas: don't wait until you're big to go to Europe and America — go there first to get big
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.description: Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and America once they're big, but it's exactly the reverse — you go there to become big. Get the region choice wrong and the later product 3.0 and channel pyramid won't stand up.
item.content:encoded:
Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and America once they're big, but it's exactly the reverse — you go there to become big. Get the region choice wrong and the later product 3.0 and channel pyramid won't stand up.

Wei Zhe compresses ten years of overseas investment experience into four choices, counterintuitive but each backed by cases and numbers, especially the second half on AI transforming organizations and pricing, which has the highest information density.

1:30 The old cross-border big-seller path is dead
Wei Zhe says the ‘cross-border big seller’ popular in Shenzhen is a distribution-type mindset, with dozens or hundreds of accounts; he has seen companies with over a thousand accounts and hundreds of thousands of SKUs. A decade ago these companies made money faster than other paths, and many investors liked them. But a distribution-type company is essentially a traffic-type company: the more stores, the more likely to get traffic. When platforms didn't have enough goods, distribution wasn't opposed; once goods are plentiful, using distribution to grab traffic is bad money driving out good. More critically, three red lines: goods not matching descriptions harms consumers, fake orders harm other merchants, and inserting cards to build private domains harms the platform. Amazon's flywheel places great importance on consumer experience, and these behaviors hit that protective wall head-on.

4:38 Four choices, region comes first
Wei Zhe says it's not just cross-border e-commerce; all of life is about choices being more important than effort. He gives four choices: region, channel, product category, and brand positioning. On region, he has always advocated seizing the European and American markets first, because of strong purchasing power, high internet penetration, and more importantly, the brand can build momentum. This isn't their invention; when Japanese and Korean brands went global, they all seized Europe and America. On category, they change their advice every three years: the first three years supported products common to China and abroad, where the domestic supply chain could sell overseas without modification, like Anker's power banks, which were almost identical except for voltage; the second three years they advised overseas-exclusive products, because China's supply chain had gone overseas and common products had no differentiation; the most recent three years is product 3.0 — electrified, with chips, with algorithms.

12:29 It's not that you go to Europe and America after getting big; you get big by going there
Many companies tell Wei Zhe ‘I'll go to Europe and America when I'm big’, and he says it's exactly the reverse: you go to Europe and America to become big. He cites Cupshe, a swimwear company, a husband and wife team who stocked $50,000 worth of goods and their first stop was the US. $50,000 is sales goods, actually very little, so there's no minimum threshold. He recently looked at AI smart hardware, starting from Kickstarter crowdfunding with a thousand or ten thousand products, even taking pre-orders before placing orders, with no capital — that's also a good way to test the waters. He even advises big companies entering the European and American markets to learn from small startups. They always say the needle must be fine enough to pierce, and both big and small companies should first do the four singles well: single market, single category, single channel, single brand.

20:36 After AI, good companies don't just find demand, they create it
Wei Zhe says with AI, excellent companies don't look for demand; they should lead demand and create demand. He cites a Chinese company making astronomical telescopes: originally not electrified, they electrified it, added chips and algorithms; the algorithm is actually simple, with GPS positioning, and the map of the universe's movements is regular. He, not originally an astronomy enthusiast, would buy one; at home in Silicon Valley, with one tap, it automatically aligns Orion for you, tells you 3 a.m. is the best time, you set it and go to sleep, and the next day it takes the photos for you. This lets everyone become a good astronomy enthusiast. Another example: a cross-border class student making curtains, after electrification they didn't sell well in the US because American electricians are expensive, so he put solar panels on the window, turning electric curtains that required an electrician into DIY ones; revenue went from one or two hundred million to four or five hundred million, with profit of one or two hundred million.

24:48 In the AI era, still using subscription fees means you're behind
Wei Zhe says in the AI era, if you still think in terms of subscription fees, you're behind again; they are all advising companies to do back-end charging, software charging, called tokenized. A monthly subscription fee is the dumbest way, a bit like advertising charging by time instead of usage. This time AI has brought out the most ideal charging model in all of human education: paying according to your usage of AI software, services, or content. He gives an example: Bessie, if you take two weeks off this month, a monthly subscription wastes two weeks. They suggest that AI-transformed hardware should be charged like AI, not the old SaaS $9.9 per month subscription model. An AI reading platform he looked at charges by how many articles you read, and nothing if you don't read; the same for smart bike trainers, after recharging, one dollar per ride, two dollars for two hours.

27:28 Adding AI is more promising than AI adding
Wei Zhe has a view called AI plus or plus AI; he reverses the phrase and is more optimistic about plus AI rather than today's AI plus. The difference: plus AI is hardware humans have already accepted, which you AI-ify; rather than creating a hardware never seen before because of AI. It's very hard for humans to accept a completely new hardware. For example, Oura makes rings, because you first accepted rings; some things that hang a camera under your neck are harder for me, I haven't accepted that hardware. So they are very optimistic about adding AI to already-accepted hardware. They invested in a capacitive stylus that is number one globally, because everyone already writes on a Pad, it doesn't add an extra pen, it just AI-ifies your pen. He also particularly wants to transform a top-two overseas fitness equipment company, replacing the fitness coach on the screen with AI-generated ones, you want a male, it's male, you want a black person, it's black, and with two cameras it can provide AI fitness guidance.

29:43 Channels are not flat; they are a pyramid
Wei Zhe says channels are not multiple channels multiple paths, each channel parallel or even competing; excellent brands all have a channel pyramid. Like luxury brands and traditional brands, there must be different channel strategies, pricing strategies, and which channel to launch new products in first. What is a light-goods channel, what is the main waist volume channel, the pyramid design differs for different categories and brands. He cites Anker: making power bank mecha seems a bit low, to enter the consumer electronics high ground of Soundcore earphones you have to get into Apple flagship stores; whether it really sells a lot doesn't matter, but it can transform the brand, Apple is the pyramid's top. Pop Mart must open on London's Oxford Street, even if it doesn't make money, how much can it lose, but it must be propped up there. He says some companies treat Temu and AliExpress as parallel channels to sell goods, which definitely won't work; AliExpress is a light-goods channel, when Amazon delists you, you dump there, you can't sell on Amazon and here too, consumers get confused.

36:14 R&D is 1, marketing is 0
Wei Zhe says he really dislikes spending heavily on marketing. Many Chinese brands going overseas or cross-border e-commerce are willing to add 2% of revenue to marketing expenses, but consumers don't get it. He says, do you dare to add 2% of revenue to R&D expenses? He has met many bosses with 1 billion or 2 billion scale; at 1 billion, they say 20 million for R&D, I don't know what for. He says, see, there's the problem, you don't know what for. Your 2% spent on marketing makes the platform happy, consumers don't get it; but 2% into R&D, consumers get it. He has always firmly believed good products speak for themselves, marketing is just, your R&D is 1, marketing is 0, if you have a good thing you can amplify it, if you don't have that 1, never put many 0s. He gives three judgment signals: first, dare to find a benchmark company, definitely a mid-to-upper brand, and you crush it by doubling performance; second, you sell at the same high price as it; third, you sell online, and offline channels come to you.

item.title: AI Office Hype Hasn't Settled, and the Personal Agent War Has Already Begun | Breaking Down Town, Instinct, Grok Bot and Muse
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-luanfanshu-10万用户估值100亿-个人agent的估值跑在产品前面/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-luanfanshu-10万用户估值100亿-个人agent的估值跑在产品前面/
item.description: Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and its product isn't even officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal agent hype, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.
item.content:encoded:
Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and its product isn't even officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal agent hype, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.

Four frontline product people break down four paths — Town, Instinct, Grok Bot, Muse — and also explain why that batch of products like Xiaolongxia became martyrs. Information density is high, but the second half is worth more.

0:00 100,000 users support a $10 billion valuation
Instinct only began small-scale invite testing in February this year, and by the end of August it still hadn't reached 100,000 users, yet its valuation rose from $50 million at the start of the year to $500 million in August, then $2.5 billion at the end of August, and this month the market is circulating a new round priced at $10 billion, with Sequoia and Benchmark both in talks to lead. The founder is a 23-year-old unknown with no big-company experience, no technical patents, no industry background. Pan Luan (潘乱) put it bluntly: what capital is buying is neither the entrepreneur nor the product, it's the story of the next OpenAI, and it can pay the price of the next-generation personal operating system to grab a ticket.

15:16 The line between tool and person is initiative
The biggest difference between this wave of agents and the last is that it is no longer another tool, but a person. Two differences between a person and a tool: first, long-term understanding — a tool needs the context explained again every time, while a person understands what kind of person you are like a friend or colleague; second, initiative — in Manus, setting up an automated task still depends on a prompt, on you spelling out the rules and intent, and that isn't initiative. True initiative is subjective agency — like the colleague who understands your goal in doing something and proactively comes over to say, "I have a plan, should we discuss it?"

18:09 Office agents organize by project, personal agents organize by person
The core difference is the dimension along which context is built. Cloud Code builds context along a mission or project dimension, and switching to the next project means starting over; this wave of personal agents builds context centered on you as a person, knowing your profile, preferences and past history. Open Codex or Manus and the list on the left is all the tasks and projects you've sent out; open Grok Bot and beside you are AI companions you can drive together. In personal scenarios, people care less about model capability and the harness layer, because individuals don't have that many complex tasks; office agents are the ones that really care about task completion rates.

30:28 Town first trades email for the user's right to delegate
The four products are trying to solve the same problem, just with different approaches. Town has a mobile app, but 70% of its data traffic is on PC; it focuses on the email scenario, solving one high-frequency scenario well before expanding. It understands which emails you send and receive often, auto-archives, learns your writing style, drafts replies for you, and sends automatically after you click confirm. Its email scenario is deeper than any other agent's, and it has already achieved fairly viral spread overseas, especially in school-related scenarios. In one sentence: use a high-frequency scenario to build user trust, and bit by bit acquire the user's ultimate right to delegate.

39:33 Poke didn't take off, and it wasn't a technical limit
Poke and Instinct are both agents that live inside IM and don't make standalone apps, but Poke didn't take off. Suki believes it wasn't a technical limit — Browser Use was already very mature by the end of last year, and Poke could have done it completely at the time; the difference was team strategy: Instinct went deeper in the agent direction, taking the full-delegation route, able to connect to credit cards, screens and microphones, booking flights and buying things for you — things users had never seen, which produced viral spread; Poke put its energy into content push accuracy, taking the proactive-push route, with email notifications arriving even earlier than the inbox itself, but it didn't take the step of "finishing the thing for you."

42:39 Cloud agents have to handle three environments
Mark says building cloud agents was a painful lesson: local agents and cloud agents are completely different things. To build personal AI you have to be usable anytime, anywhere — you can't be unreachable just because the computer screen is off. The cloud has to handle three environments — the user's device, the cloud service, and the agent's execution environment — and task state, task interruption and recovery, and context transfer between the three are very complex systems. They started in February, and just getting the agent to run stably in the cloud took at least two months; excluding detours, polishing a sincere piece of work takes at least three to four months.

50:39 Hiring an assistant and being a middleman are two businesses
Town started out doing corporate tax filing, and after pivoting it leans more toward enterprise scenarios; the relationship is more like you paying to hire a personal assistant, which naturally filters for people willing to pay, with a typical profile of white-collar workers who are extremely busy and have no time or energy. Muse is more like a middleman, shopping guide or broker; although it has a paid subscription, the main projected revenue source is still commission from matching transactions, leaning toward mass users and blending into everyday WhatsApp chats. Two completely different logics, cutting different scenarios and filtering out different users.

1:14:07 For an agent, the saved folder may be noise
The story Zuckerberg told when launching Muse was about extracting what you like to eat from ingredients saved on Instagram, generating a shopping list, adjusting the menu by dinner party size and dietary restrictions, then completing the shopping and relationship maintenance — turning years of interest profile into money, going from a discovery platform to a decision-and-transaction platform. But Suki suspects this is to save face for the free business narrative: helping users complete transactions is absolutely not among the top scenarios users want to solve; users would rather solve the annoying things they don't want to do themselves. There isn't that much high-quality context in saved folders; truly high-quality context comes more from offline, IM and email, and Douyin and Instagram saves may themselves be noise to an agent.

item.title: Ten Years of Parenting Taught Me: When Your Kid Won't Listen, the Problem Isn't Your Kid
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-parentmojo-育儿十年才懂-孩子不听话时-问题不在孩子身上/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-parentmojo-育儿十年才懂-孩子不听话时-问题不在孩子身上/
item.description: On the podcast's tenth anniversary, the host revisits ten parenting beliefs she once held as certain — from forcing her daughter to take medicine to treating an expert's framework as gospel — each one first learned in a book, then relearned in a real conflict.
item.content:encoded:
On the podcast's tenth anniversary, the host revisits ten parenting beliefs she once held as certain — from forcing her daughter to take medicine to treating an expert's framework as gospel — each one first learned in a book, then relearned in a real conflict.

For parents who want to interrogate their own parenting methodology. Medium information density, heavy on personal narrative, but the ten reflections are clearly structured, and the back half — on the ‘village’ and the couple relationship — is more valuable than the front half.

6:00 Forcing the medicine won the behavior and lost the relationship
The host recalls her three-year-old daughter refusing antibiotics; she held her down and forced the medicine in, and her daughter threw most of it back up. That night her husband Alvin stayed with their daughter in the bathroom for an hour, calmly saying the whole time, ‘I'm willing to do anything, but we're not leaving until we figure this out,’ and in the end the daughter finished the whole course herself, with small sips of medicine, small sips of water, and a small piece of chocolate to take the taste away. The host says the difference wasn't that her husband was more patient — it's that he wasn't solving a behavior, he was understanding what would actually help the child do this thing. What the child needed was autonomy over the process, and to feel that she and her parent were on the same team, rather than being held down to do something.

9:19 The authoritative parenting framework rests on 146 white kids
The host says she accepted uncritically early on that ‘authoritative is the best parenting style,’ because every blog and every study said so.
