It wasn't until she made the episode on corporal punishment that she found a paper co-authored by Diana Baumrind defending parents' ability to spank their children, and started digging. She found that this framework — cited more than 26,000 times and defining sixty years of parenting research — was originally based on just 146 white, middle-class preschoolers in the town where Baumrind lived. She calls this evidence of her own insufficient critical thinking, and says she now asks at the macro level ‘does this theory make sense,’ and at the micro level ‘does it fit this specific child in front of me.’

17:41 Not punishing your kid doesn't mean being ruled by your kid
The host says she once believed that without punishments and consequences children would run wild — she was even in the shower when her daughter was four months old thinking ‘how do I discipline her without becoming a mean mom.’ Clinical psychologist Dr. Houri Parsi admitted in the membership community that she too had treated ‘obedience’ as the goal, and that every tooth-brushing was a battle. Once, recording for the host to see, she deliberately withheld threats, punishments and rewards and simply asked her two-year-old son ‘why don't you want to brush your teeth.’ He couldn't find the words, just called out for mama and buried his head in her chest — she realized what he wanted was time alone with her. She put the toilet lid down, sat down, held her son, and sang a song with him, and he brushed his teeth himself, the whole thing in under five minutes.

21:31 ‘I need you to take out the trash’ is not a need
The host says that looking back, she didn't understand what a ‘need’ was — she thought saying ‘I need you to take out the trash’ to her husband was a perfectly logical sentence. Before their daughter was born the two of them almost never argued: mountain biking in summer, skiing in winter, because the ad agency they worked for represented resorts and paid them in vouchers. After their daughter was born everything changed: during his three weeks of paternity leave her husband would fetch her anything she wanted, and the rest of the time he was training for a hundred-mile ride and watching the Tour de France. She says it was learning that she had needs for ‘collaboration, partnership, effort being seen’ that actually pried open the problems between them; before that she carried a large amount of resentment inside her with no idea how to handle it.

24:01 When you're triggered, the problem isn't the person who interrupted you
The host says her biggest trigger is being interrupted — the moment her husband interrupts her she flies into a rage, most recently over how much postage a package needed. She always assumed the cause was simply that her husband interrupted her, and that if he stopped, everything would be fine. In July 2018, recording with intergenerational trauma expert Dr. Rebecca Babcock-Fenerci, she traced it live to her own father, a special education teacher who would treat sixteen-year-olds like ten-year-olds and who for a stretch lectured her every night. Later, in the car, she interrupted her daughter, and her daughter said ‘don't interrupt me, Mama,’ and her husband looked at her and said ‘she is you.’ She says that was the moment she realized this had never been only about the two people in the room, and out of it she developed the ‘Tame Your Triggers’ course, which grew from a one-month module to ten weeks.

30:27 The handmade book she made while pregnant was full of expectations for her child
The host describes a book she made while pregnant: three covers, one in the middle and one on each side, opening in both directions, brown book cloth with a beige spine, the word ‘me’ cut out of the board on one cover, and on the reverse cover the word ‘you’ embossed, the concept being ‘you came out of me.’ On the ‘me’ side she wrote her own feelings and thoughts; on the ‘you’ side she wrote to the Carys she had not yet met. She reads out the earliest batch of ‘expectations for you’: I hope you're smart, or at least average; I hope you're the kind of child who shakes hands with people instead of hiding behind my legs; I hope you like both roughhousing and pretty things; I hope you don't cry all the time; I hope when you fall you pick yourself up and say ‘I'm okay.’ She says looking back now, her biggest mistake was not knowing how to simply be with a person, to let them be their whole self and witness it, without carrying ideas about how they should be.

33:14 Kohn's principle two: reconsider your demands first
The host says she once assumed she'd play the role of ‘enforcer,’ and even wrote ‘I hope you can love me the way he does’ on her pregnancy expectations list. She says RIE loosened the soil for her, but what actually planted the seed was Alfie Kohn's Unconditional Parenting. She shares a few of its principles: principle two is to reconsider your demands — ‘maybe when a child won't do what you ask, the problem isn't the child, it's what you're asking’; principle five is to change how you look, not just how you act — when you see your child doing the thing you asked them not to do, your first reaction should be curiosity about what they're struggling with, not how to make them stop; principle ten is ‘attribute to your child the best motive consistent with the observed facts,’ and she says when she quotes it she changes the ending to ‘consistent with the observed behavior,’ because ‘there are no facts, only what we observe.’

39:07 The couple relationship isn't a separate subject, it's the same one
The host says she long believed the couple relationship and the parent-child relationship were completely different things — when she started the parenting membership eight years ago she asked Dr. Laura Froyen to write the co-parenting module, because she had no idea how to handle a partner relationship. She says her parenting shift toward collaboration was relatively easy, because she had no ten-year-old habits with her daughter; but with Alvin she'd been together ten years and had never learned how to disagree, because most of that time was spent doing hobbies they loved, and she didn't mind doing most of the housework. It wasn't until she took Gottman training that she realized this was almost the same work she'd been doing with her child all these years — while also believing the Gottman method itself has a few key flaws. She recruited couples from the membership to record real arguments, using modified tools, and one couple — where the husband had refused to discuss a toxic issue — became willing to talk after his wife listened for ten minutes with a genuine intent to understand him, and in that same session they reached an agreement to move forward.

item.title: NPR's comment section was mistaken for bots — it was actually a group of middle schoolers
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-tal-npr-评论区被当成机器人-其实是一群初中生/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-tal-npr-评论区被当成机器人-其实是一群初中生/
item.description: NPR staff saw a pile of gibberish in the comments and their first instinct was bots, so they reported it. A younger colleague recognized it as kids whose parents had blocked social media, using a Spotify comment section as a group chat.
item.content:encoded:
NPR staff saw a pile of gibberish in the comments and their first instinct was bots, so they reported it. A younger colleague recognized it as kids whose parents had blocked social media, using a Spotify comment section as a group chat.

Four independent stories, medium information density, but the generational misread in the first story and the mother-daughter conversation about braiding in the third are both worth hearing.

1:01 The gibberish comments aren't bots, they're kids
Dave Blanchard saw a sudden flood of incomprehensible messages in the Wild Card comment section on Spotify, and his first instinct was bots, so he reported them to Spotify and had the posts deleted. But Hannah Chin, a colleague at NPR ten years younger, opened the screenshots and immediately reached the opposite conclusion: these are kids. Her evidence was the display names full of emoji you need a special character generator to type, the unfamiliar cartoon avatars, and the back-and-forth short sentences with piles of exclamation marks. Dave wasn't buying it at first, and replied, "That's an interesting theory."

6:05 Using a playlist as the group chat entrance
Hannah kept digging and found how the kids did it: one kid creates a public playlist called Let's Chat Here or New Chat with just one podcast episode in it; other kids see the playlist, click into that episode, and chat in the comments. They also posted Google Forms as little quizzes, writing "only cool people can fill this out." Hannah said bots don't go post Google Forms, but Gen Alpha does, the same way her generation made their own personality quizzes on UQuiz or BuzzFeed. That was the message that convinced Dave.

8:06 They picked NPR because the comments were empty
The show reached out to several commenters, and only one, a 14-year-old girl named Ella, agreed to be interviewed; she did the interview from the car while her father drove. Ella said the core of the group is about 20 kids, many of them in drama club, mostly girls, with strict parents who don't let them use regular social media. They first chatted in the comment section of a podcast that played TikTok videos, and after that podcast got shut down, the kids started using playlists to move to new territory. Asked why they chose NPR shows, Ella said: we look for podcasts that don't have many comments, so we don't get mixed up in other people's comments.

11:08 Dave needed a generational translator
After learning the truth, Dave said he felt guilty for reporting them, and also felt old. He said, "I literally needed Hannah to be my generational translator," and that this made him acutely aware of his age and how out of date he was. Ella said she's sure that one day she'll be just like Dave and understand nothing. The show puts this segment at the top, as the entry point to the whole episode's theme of "intergenerational space travel."

25:35 The wedding toast was a poem nobody understood
At 18, Courtney read a poem she wrote at her mother's second wedding, and her mother held it against her for thirty years. The poem opens with the mother walking in habitual darkness, every breath like her last, moves to the mother standing by the counter smoking, and then turns at the end toward "you found roots, you found a soul worth worshipping." The mother said that on the wedding day she only heard the negative first half and never heard the kindness at the end; rereading it, Courtney admitted that presenting a bride with that dark a picture on her wedding day really would make it impossible to hear the good part.

31:52 The body knew the marriage was wrong first
Two days after the wedding, the 49-year-old mother suffered a massive stroke. Courtney offers a theory: her mother's body, not her mind, had known all along that the marriage was a mistake. The mother agreed, saying she knew when she was buying the wedding dress, that she wasn't all that happy then, that she "anticipated this awfulness ahead of time," sensing it in every fiber. This exchange turns all the earlier arguing about the wedding toast into a question about why her mother didn't listen to her intuition back then.

39:05 Getting rid of the stepfather is what repaired them
Last October, the mother fell in the kitchen Mr. X designed and broke her back; Mr. X was too drunk to help, and only hours later handed her the phone so she could call an ambulance herself. The mother was hospitalized for months and gave Courtney power of attorney to go to court and get Mr. X out. Courtney said it was the hardest thing she's ever done, but they won. The mother said it was precisely because Courtney spent so much time here for that, that she realized how much her daughter cared about her. Mr. X drove them apart, and getting rid of him pulled them back together.

55:41 The mother says braiding shouldn't be the entry to toughness
Myra Flynn locks horns with her six-year-old daughter Avalon every morning over braiding, and she blurted out "sometimes what we need isn't comfortable," then immediately realized those were her own mother's words. She called her mother, Martha Mathis, expecting support, but her mother said: braiding shouldn't be the entry point for making a kid tough, because it carries too many racial and gender meanings; and six-year-old Avalon is already the toughest little girl there is. Her mother's advice was to let Avalon handle a small section of hair herself, because "she'll be gentle with herself."

item.title: Robots Are Still at GPT-1, and the Real Signal Is Success Rate, Not Loss
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-crossing-机器人还在-gpt-1-阶段-真正的信号是成功率不是-loss/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-crossing-机器人还在-gpt-1-阶段-真正的信号是成功率不是-loss/
item.description: The Scaling Law signal for embodied intelligence has already appeared, but we're measuring the wrong thing: low loss doesn't mean high success rate, and fitting the 17 steps that never touch the object is meaningless.
item.content:encoded:
The Scaling Law signal for embodied intelligence has already appeared, but we're measuring the wrong thing: low loss doesn't mean high success rate, and fitting the 17 steps that never touch the object is meaningless.

Xu Mengdi, assistant professor at Tsinghua's Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences, on data, world models and In-Context Learning for embodied intelligence — the middle and later sections on the data loop and the loss trap are the most valuable.

12:15 Pretraining isn't everything — adaptation is what's missing
Xu Mengdi's CMU best doctoral thesis is titled Building Adaptable Generalist Robots, and its core claim is: pretraining is extremely useful, but you can't expect a robot to succeed 100% of the time on pretraining alone. The defining feature of the open world is that tasks keep changing — a home has 20 objects today, a week later it has 30 of different kinds, and people's preferences shift too. So the robot has to be able to adapt to change in its deployment environment and improve itself. She explored two routes: In-Context Learning and test-time training, the latter changing only 0.5% of the adapter parameters — but change too much and it forgets what it learned in pretraining.

19:22 Why adaptation only started to matter now
Humans generalise well for two reasons: extremely strong priors, and the ability to learn things very fast. The mainstream approach until now has been to scale data and models so that multi-task and instruction-following abilities get stronger — essentially giving the model a strong enough prior first. But Xu Mengdi points out this doesn't mean adaptation is unimportant — it's just that people only recently realised it. And adaptation places demands on the base model: you don't want the robot's self-learning process in a real setting to be terrifying, like smashing a cup. So starting from pretraining is reasonable.

49:46 Low loss does not mean high success rate
This is the most counterintuitive technical judgment in the whole piece. There's a very tricky point in robotics: loss is not directly tied to success rate. Loss can be very low while the final success rate is not necessarily low — there's a lot of oscillation. Her example: a task might take 20 steps in total, and the first 17 steps involve no contact with the object at all. Even if those 17 steps fit extremely well, if step 18 — the one that actually touches the object — has a relatively large error, the task fails easily. This is an imbalance in the time sequence. So the Scaling Law that actually means something should be: as data gradually increases and the model gradually grows, success rate on unseen tasks gradually rises.

50:47 Robots are still at the GPT-1 moment
Today's mainstream embodied models are still ‘pretraining + fine-tuning on the target domain’, which is analogous to the GPT-1 stage of language models — GPT-1 itself also needed targeted post-training to solve the corresponding tasks. What Xu Mengdi really wants to reach is the GPT-3 moment: giving the model task information through ICL, through prompting, with no fine-tuning needed — telling the model what to do purely through context. That way fine-tuning's share drops even lower, and it becomes easier to scale to more scenarios and complete more tasks, so ordinary people can use it too.

58:49 The data loop is a chicken-and-egg problem
The hardest point is whether you can give the model a stable data loop. That requires putting the robot into end-user homes or service scenarios, having a suitable mentor to teach it, and having the robot show obvious progress after half an hour of teaching — only then will end users be willing to use it, and only then does the data loop start turning. But there's a chicken-and-egg problem here: the base model needs to be good enough and learn fast enough, yet the model also needs to get into the scenario first so users start using it, in order to draw out that base capability. So whether the data loop can be made to work is the riskiest point of all.

1:03:52 Data is defined backwards from model capability
Data itself gets fed to the model, but the definition of data isn't conjured out of thin air — it's defined by the model's capabilities. When people define data, what they're actually doing is: figuring out what capabilities the model needs, and working backwards to how the data should be collected. If you need smoother motion, the data has to be the smooth kind; if you need fail-recovery ability, the data has to be collected with failures and corrections in it. And right now people's definition of model capability is still fairly vague, so the data requirements are vague too.

1:05:54 Four kinds of data, each with its own place
Xu Mengdi's position is fusion, because different data teaches the model different things. Teleoperation data is closest to the robot body itself, suited to the later training stage, making the model more directly relevant to the target domain. Simulation data easily produces position generalisation and texture generalisation, making the model more robust to visual change, suited to pretraining or the front end of mid-training. UMI data sits in the middle, more like robot data but cheaper to collect. Human data is the cheapest, can be spread widely across different scenarios, and what it teaches is scene variation and task-relevant information, less tied to the specific shape of the morphology.

1:19:02 AI-written papers are obvious at a glance
Robotics papers have been doubling recently, and Xu Mengdi's way of coping is to scroll through articles promoted by the researchers she follows, because the author list itself has already done a layer of filtering. She can clearly see that some articles have a very large AI-written component. Her judgment: AI-written articles may pass review and actually get into some conferences, but overall the quality still won't be higher than human-written ones, because they look familiar while in fact many of the arguments are riddled with holes and there isn't much content. Once she finds out a paper was AI-written, her interest in it is discounted.

item.title: Intel's Optane Died Because 3D NAND Was Too Cheap, Not Because the Tech Was Bad
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-asianometry-intel-的-optane-死于-3d-nand-太便宜-不是技术不行/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-asianometry-intel-的-optane-死于-3d-nand-太便宜-不是技术不行/
item.description: Phase-change memory was worked on from 1970 to 2022, and every time it got squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.
item.content:encoded:
Phase-change memory was worked on from 1970 to 2022, and every time it got squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.

A complete failure history of a memory technology, from RMM in 1970 to the Optane shutdown in 2022. Medium information density; the back half on data-center deployment and Micron's exit is the most valuable part.

3:07 The physics of phase-change memory is what makes it slow
Phase-change memory stores data by switching a material between a crystalline and an amorphous state: the crystalline state has low resistance, the amorphous state high resistance, and the two differ by three to four orders of magnitude. Melting the material and quenching it into the amorphous state is called RESET; the reverse is called SET. SET either melts the material into a liquid and lets it cool slowly into a crystal, or heats it to a temperature high enough to convert it directly to crystal without melting. The author points out that SET is often the speed bottleneck for PCM. This physical mechanism has not changed since Stanford Ovshinsky discovered the phase-change behavior of chalcogenide compounds in the 1960s.

4:13 Intel built phase-change memory in 1970, then forgot
In 1970, RG Neale and DL Nelson of Energy Conversion Devices and Intel's Gordon Moore published an article in Electronics magazine announcing "Read-Mostly Memory," positioned between RAM and ROM, for storing data that programs read often but rarely change. Each cell was a silicon diode plus a layer of phase-change material; Intel supplied the silicon substrate, ECD supplied the material. But in 1970 the minimum feature size was only 10 microns, power consumption was high, SET took milliseconds, and endurance was low. DRAM capacity was growing, EPROM arrived, and RMM disappeared. Years later, when someone asked the 79-year-old Moore about the article, he said he had no memory of it at all.

9:25 Numonyx treated PCM as its only shot at a comeback
The rise of NAND sent NOR flash into a long decline, and in 2007 global NOR sales fell 9% year over year. Intel merged its NOR business with STMicroelectronics' flash business, forming the Swiss company Numonyx in 2008, with an investment from Francisco Partners and a bank loan. NOR had none of NAND's growth prospects, so Numonyx could only bet on PCM — PCM combined NOR's fast random reads with NAND's high-capacity storage, and in theory could replace both. In February 2008 Intel announced delivery of its first PCM prototype, Alverstone, at 128 megabit and 90 nanometers.

13:33 Mobile PCM was swept away in one wave by 3D NAND
PCM's entry strategy was to attack the mobile market, replacing the NOR flash that stores boot code while also storing data. In 2009 Samsung announced a 512 megabit PRAM at 60 nanometers, saying that paired with DRAM it could save more than 20% in power. Micron acquired Numonyx in 2010 for about $1.2 billion in stock, and in July 2012 finally shipped 1 gigabit PCM at 45 nanometers, which Nokia put into its Asha feature phones. But in August 2013 Samsung announced mass production of 24-layer 3D NAND, and 3D NAND then set off the steepest cost-decline curve in semiconductor history, and mobile PCM's most compelling rationale was gone. In January 2014 Micron announced it was pulling out of mobile PCM.

17:38 Intel and Micron were split on Optane's positioning from the start
In July 2018 Intel and Micron agreed to a friendly split, going their separate ways after completing joint development of second-generation 3D XPoint. The disagreement was over product direction: Intel initially aimed Optane SSDs at consumer PCs and laptops, hoping to spread wafer costs across volume; Micron wanted to go straight into the data center. Jon Carter hinted back in 2016 that consumer systems did not really need 3D XPoint's low latency, non-volatility and endurance, or at least not enough to pay four to five times the price of NAND for them. In October 2018 Micron announced it would pay $1.5 billion to buy Intel's half of the IM Flash plant in Utah, and Intel shifted to producing it itself.

22:47 Putting Optane in the data center meant redoing motherboards and software
In April 2019 the first DIMM-form-factor Optane DC Persistent Memory went on sale, four years after 3D XPoint was announced, and it required matching Xeon processors, chipsets and motherboards. It had two modes: Memory Mode pooled Optane and DRAM into a single volatile memory pool, worked out of the box, but its value depended on DRAM price swings; App Direct Mode was the genuinely valuable mode, letting software write persistent data into Optane so it was still there after a reboot. Restarting an Oracle or SAP database usually takes more than an hour to reload data from SSDs or disks, and Optane could eliminate that. One imprecise but directionally useful test showed a 12.5x improvement. But App Direct Mode required programmers to rethink data consistency.

24:51 Only 40% of 582 proofs of concept used the mode that actually mattered
In 2020 Intel updated Optane adoption, saying there were 582 proofs of concept in the pipeline, with SAP HANA and Oracle Exadata as the main users and the rest mostly in high-performance computing, infrastructure and some AI analytics. But only 40% used the more valuable App Direct Mode. Intel said it believed the industry would eventually adopt that mode, but it might take years. In the same period Intel announced the sale of its 3D NAND business to SK hynix for $9 billion, with Optane not part of the deal — seemingly an endorsement, but it also let people infer that Optane's implied loss in 2020 was more than $500 million.

25:52 After Micron left, Optane had only a single supplier
In March 2021 Micron announced it was immediately stopping 3D XPoint development, saying the Utah plant had long suffered from underutilization and dragged $400 million a year off the company, and the plant was later sold to Texas Instruments. Micron attributed the decision to 3D NAND prices continuing to fall, and to the hard changes data centers and applications would have to make to take full advantage of the product. Micron pivoted to betting on the open-standard interface CXL, because machine-learning systems made Micron realize that not just CPUs needed more memory — GPUs and AI accelerator ASICs did too. Micron's public exit severely weakened Optane: customers could rely only on Intel as a single source, and Optane was a proprietary technology. In July 2022, on its earnings call, Intel quietly announced it was shutting down the Optane business.

item.title: Huawei's Ascend chose the hardest road: not compatible with Nvidia
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-touzishizhan-华为昇腾选了一条最难的路-不兼容英伟达/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-touzishizhan-华为昇腾选了一条最难的路-不兼容英伟达/
item.description: For three or four decades Chinese IT has been a follower. Ascend is Huawei's first product that doesn't solve a chokehold problem but instead goes into uncharted territory, starting at the same time as Nvidia. Xu Zhijun said: anything you do as a follower gets harder and harder the longer you do it.
item.content:encoded:
For three or four decades Chinese IT has been a follower. Ascend is Huawei's first product that doesn't solve a chokehold problem but instead goes into uncharted territory, starting at the same time as Nvidia. Xu Zhijun said: anything you do as a follower gets harder and harder the longer you do it.

The first half is about how the book was written, with low information density; from the two key decisions at Ascend's founding onward, Fang Xingdong gives a lot of first-hand detail and judgment that only appears in the book.

16:10 Ascend's harshest decision was not being compatible with Nvidia
At Ascend's founding there were two choices. The first was whether AI chips should be specialized or general-purpose; Liao Heng, as chief scientist, judged that AI should be a general-purpose product, and the architecture choice has been proven right today. The second was harder: whether to be compatible with Nvidia. Many domestic chips chose compatibility, with the benefit that Nvidia's existing ecosystem and tools could all be shared. But Xu Zhijun was firm from the start that they must blaze a different trail. Fang Xingdong believes this choice was extremely bold at the time, and that many times along the way it faced enormous challenges — because the entire Chinese IT industry has been a follower industry for three or four decades, and has never developed based on its own root technologies.

19:11 Anything you do as a follower gets harder and harder
Fang Xingdong recalls having dinner with Xu Zhijun three years ago, when Xu half muttered to himself: Huawei has done this for so many years, and the discovery is that anything you do as a follower always gets harder and harder the longer you do it. There are two kinds of following: in standardized products, Chinese companies can always close the gap and even overtake, but by the time they overtake, there is no profit left in the industry — 2G to 5G, PCs, phones all went this way; in non-standardized areas, such as competing with Cisco in routers for so many years, the gap has not closed. In Xu Zhijun's eyes, what Huawei did in the past was also following. So Ascend is special among the six products: the other five solve chokeholds and address survival first, while Ascend was not choked in 2019 — it is a fully proactive compute product.

29:16 With process choked off, only system innovation can make it back
Each generation of industry chips gains roughly 20% or more in performance, mainly from the increase in transistor count driven by advanced process improvements. Huawei lost this premise and can only gain performance through system innovation and breakthroughs — stacked compute, interconnect, higher integration. Fang Xingdong explains with a car metaphor: before, you just had to make the engine stronger and stronger; now the engine is constrained and can no longer be enlarged, so you can only make the car run well through architecture, weight reduction, heat dissipation and other factors. Nvidia's solution is to keep working on the engine, because TSMC can still manufacture it. In the interview Liao Heng uses the metaphor of an 18-story pagoda: many companies are good at only one layer because of the great division of labor, while Huawei is forced to do manufacturing, ecosystem and chip design all at once.

34:21 Huawei has to pull the domestic supply chain up with it
Previously Huawei did design, relied on the global supply chain, had TSMC manufacture, could choose the best international partners for other components, directly buy American products and assemble them, sell at a good price with a brand premium, and make decent profit. Now it cannot cooperate with foreign partners, TSMC cannot process for it, and domestic processes are still lacking in every respect, so Huawei has no choice but to support and pull up the domestic supply chain — only then does it have a way to survive and get products manufactured. So the challenge of the past seven years is not just improving its own capabilities but also pulling the entire supply chain up — without that, independent self-reliance is impossible. Manufacturing is not Huawei's main business, but it has to help companies like SMIC and Yangtze Memory keep advancing process, yield and quality.

37:40 Ascend's significance is not that Huawei survives, but that the industry has an engine
In the past Huawei's product launches and iterations were still based on American root technologies and the industrial ecosystem, and the high-value components of a phone were basically foreign. Now Huawei's phones, including Ascend, almost 100% pull up the domestic supply chain. Fang Xingdong believes the greatest significance of the Tao Law is not that Huawei itself can survive and be self-reliant, but that China's entire semiconductor industry and entire IT industry have their own engine, which never existed before. Huawei's rapid development represents the rapid development of the entire industrial ecosystem. He also points out that the market, reading reports, news or public opinion, has not yet realized that we are at this inflection point in the cycle — mention Nvidia and people think it is formidable, mention Huawei and they say it is policy that makes everyone use it.

45:47 It is not a question of difficulty, but of cognition and resolve
Fang Xingdong believes doing communications versus doing IT is essentially not a question of difficulty but of cognition and resolve — whether you dare to do it. The most typical example is the GaussDB database: among these six products Ascend stood out, and the least conspicuous may be Gauss, but databases are a half-century-old industry with a fairly stable market, and being truly choked there is deadly. Huawei at the time wanted to acquire or support a domestic vendor, but after research found none was up to it — domestic companies could only grow in the cracks of American giants, with small scale, weak R&D and weak product innovation. So Huawei decided to do it itself, benchmarking Oracle, investing 1 billion, 2 billion, 3 billion yuan a year starting in 2011 and 2012, without knowing whether there would be any output in the future.

1:06:04 The future is two centers, not one replacing the other
Fang Xingdong judges that global high tech moving from a single system centered on the US to two centers is the general trend; politics will not allow a continued single center — the US will not allow it, and China will not allow it either. He believes a single center is itself abnormal, and only two centers can create competition — only with two systems does every consumer, every company, every country, no matter how big or small, have a choice, and not be choked into a forced either-or. So the mission of Huawei's six products is to go from being the second choice to being the better choice; the relationship with Nvidia is not simple substitution but each having its strengths, complementing each other, and co-opetition. He admits the American system is currently stronger, with its advantage mainly in advanced manufacturing, and that Huawei, under process constraints, relies on the Tao Law to avoid being left behind; once advanced process is also broken through, it can work both routes at once.

1:19:11 The tech war won in the short term, at a greater long-term cost
Fang Xingdong believes the US did indeed suppress Huawei through the tech war, but cannot solve the problem in the long term. He reasons: without the national confrontation of 2017 and 2018, Huawei might be at least one-third of Nvidia, one-third of Apple, and possibly China's largest company by market cap; in 2019 Huawei had already surpassed Apple, and its global shipments briefly surpassed Samsung for one quarter. Nvidia today is dominant alone; if it had been running neck and neck with Huawei in AI chips from the start, it could not be in this position today. He judges that once the side being attacked builds a self-cycle that does not rely on the outside, and the other side cannot eliminate it even under the harshest conditions, it will be even harder to eliminate later — it will only grow stronger, turning from one monopoly into two competitors.

item.title: Ads Are Machine Learning 1.0: How AppLovin Earned an 84% Margin From It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-allin-广告是机器学习的-1-0-applovin-靠它赚出-84-利润率/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-allin-广告是机器学习的-1-0-applovin-靠它赚出-84-利润率/
item.description: Advertising isn't AI's past tense — it's the earliest and most profitable deployment of deep learning. AppLovin used recommendation models to build an 84% EBITDA margin in the $50 billion mobile game ad market, and became its own best investor with $6 billion of buybacks.
item.content:encoded:
Advertising isn't AI's past tense — it's the earliest and most profitable deployment of deep learning. AppLovin used recommendation models to build an 84% EBITDA margin in the $50 billion mobile game ad market, and became its own best investor with $6 billion of buybacks.

A CEO who almost never gives interviews explains the shared technical roots of advertising and AI, the buyback playbook through a 92% drawdown, and why a Chinese engineering team is an advantage. High information density, worth listening to.

1:02 Mobile game advertising is a $50 billion market
Adam says outsiders underestimate the scale of mobile gaming: over a billion adults play casual mobile games every day, and these people are household decision-makers. Two years ago AppLovin disclosed $11 billion of annual ad spend on its own platform, and it has grown at roughly 60% year over year since, which by rough math puts it at about $20 billion today. But that isn't the whole market — many other ad companies monetize in this ecosystem, so double that number and the entire mobile game ecosystem spends roughly $50 billion a year on advertising. He notes that not long ago social was also just a $50 billion opportunity.

3:02 Advertising is machine learning's earliest and most profitable implementation
Adam calls advertising ML 1.0: it was the first deployment of all these technologies that now drive AI. Large language models create more economic value today than advertising, but advertising is an extremely profitable implementation of deep learning models. Recommendation systems and large language models have different architectures, but their trajectories are highly similar — research in large language models can transfer to recommendation systems and vice versa; many large language model researchers spent the early part of their careers looking at ad systems. The beauty of the ad business is that you build a model to predict a future outcome, and the value of that prediction can be converted into money immediately.

6:03 Search ads create no economic increment; discovery ads do
Adam splits advertising into two categories. One is bottom-of-funnel advertising: the consumer already knows what they want to buy and is just doing research to complete the transaction — that's Google Search's business, and large language models will compete with Google Search almost entirely in that area. The other is his own field: not knowing user intent, creating a demand that didn't previously exist, so the user sees it and thinks ‘this looks really cool, I want to buy it right now’. He stresses that the transaction in search or in a large language model was going to happen anyway, so there isn't much economic expansion there; discovery advertising creates economic increment, which is why Meta's ad business is so strong and what AppLovin wants to do.

8:07 Your phone isn't listening, but your behavior is tracked
Faced with the question of ‘I talk about something at lunch and then an ad for it appears’, Adam says it's more likely you did something trackable earlier — a search, a website visit, a product search — without realizing it, and then you said something related and started seeing related ads. He states plainly that AppLovin does not track location at all, arguing that tracking precise location to render ads is a very heavy concept, and that the data transfer required to parse microphone content in real time and translate it into an ad is unrealistic. But he concedes that if you're on a social network, relationship data between you and others can of course drive the ad experience — for example, a friend searched for something and you might see a related ad, which he doesn't see as a problem.

10:07 From $28 billion to $3.8 billion, then it started buying itself
AppLovin went public in April 2021 with $600 million of EBITDA at a market cap of about $28 billion, peaking at $40 billion. In 2022 the stock fell almost every day, down to a market cap of about $3.8 billion — in a year when the company did $1 billion of EBITDA. Adam's read: market cap is determined by the quality of investors, and at the time a lot of companies were going public at the same time, blue-chip investors hadn't done the research to figure out what this company with the silly name was, and the result was no demand and lots of supply, with the valuation falling from 50x EBITDA to under 4x. His response was to stop talking to investors and instead use the large amounts of cash the company generated to buy back aggressively, eventually buying about $6 billion of its own stock and retiring 20% to 25% of the shares outstanding.

12:07 When the stock fell 92%, family called to ask if you wanted to kill yourself
Adam says that period was hard, that family and friends would call to ask if he wanted to kill himself, and his answer was that the stock was still at $10 and had still gone up a lot. But the truly hard part was realizing that as CEO, his team was getting the same calls, and they didn't have his composure or his equity. So they rallied the team around a ‘we versus the world’ mentality, and extended a performance stock program usually reserved for the CEO to key people across the company, telling them: it's hard right now, the house you thought you had is gone, but if you hold on and recover, the upside is huge. Later investors started coming back, the company switched from regression models to deep learning models, the ad algorithm got better, advertiser returns got better, and the business started growing fast.

14:08 A week in New York took the market cap from $28 billion to $55 billion
When the new model launched in April 2023 the company still wasn't talking to investors, so the outside world didn't know. By around September 2023 the stock was at $80 with good results, and Adam judged the market cap high enough that it couldn't buy back that aggressively anymore, so he went to New York and started talking to investors. In that one week the stock went from $80 to $150, and the market cap from $28 billion to $55 billion — just because he went out and said ‘our company is still here, we survived’. He describes sitting in meetings and being able to read the person across the table texting a friend to buy. Over the next two and a half years the stock went from $9 to $750, a $250 billion market cap. His conclusion is that public market investors and private investors aren't that different, both chase trends, just often later than you'd like.

16:09 After privacy rules tightened, users complained ads got worse
Adam says in these areas you want regulatory clarity, and once the rules are clear, technology can respond. Five years ago you could target users precisely on iOS; today if users say no precise targeting, you can only bundle them into groups and serve worse ads. The interesting result of this change is that after Apple's change the company received a flood of user complaints saying ‘show me more relevant ads, you're showing me a bunch of junk now’. So he offers a duality: on one hand you need privacy regulation so tech companies know what to do, on the other hand consumers do want relevant ads — when you watch a 30-second ad in a game to get an extra life, you're getting something with monetary value, and you don't want to spend those 30 seconds on junk.

item.title: Buffets Weren't Eaten to Death — They Were Hollowed Out by the Supermarket Deli Counter
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-modernmba-自助餐不是被吃垮的-是被超市熟食区掏空的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-modernmba-自助餐不是被吃垮的-是被超市熟食区掏空的/
item.description: The 1980s buffet ran on cheap food, cheap land, cheap labor and stagnant wages. When all four inputs got more expensive, what actually killed it was the supermarket deli counter eating the low-price market at zero customer-acquisition cost.
item.content:encoded:
The 1980s buffet ran on cheap food, cheap land, cheap labor and stagnant wages. When all four inputs got more expensive, what actually killed it was the supermarket deli counter eating the low-price market at zero customer-acquisition cost.

It dissects an industry's cause of death using the financials and bankruptcy filings of three public companies — the mechanism is clear and the numbers are solid, and the back half on supermarket deli counters is the most valuable part.

0:02 The buffet deleted everything hard about running a restaurant
The real leap of the 1980s buffet was upgrading "unlimited" from a side dish to the entire business model. It cut every hard part of a traditional restaurant: no servers to hire, no menu to design, barely any English required, no precision needed. The only job was cooking in bulk, heating frozen appetizers and portioning factory cake. Compared with a regular restaurant where every dish has to earn back its own price, a buffet only has to keep the pans full. Lower skill threshold, a concept that sells itself, one family able to run the whole kitchen, customers serving themselves — the whole model ran on volume. Within a decade, nearly every small town in the Midwest had a Chinese buffet.

8:07 Knowing how to open stores and knowing how to keep customers are two different businesses
Buffets Inc.'s Old Country and Hometown had the simplest strategy of all: this model doesn't need improvement, it needs replication. From one store to 200 in a decade, doubling again in five years, opening more than one a week at the peak, and after the 1996 merger becoming the largest and fastest buffet operator in the world with nearly a billion dollars in annual revenue. But fast success created a fatal blind spot — they built the muscle to open buffets, not the muscle to keep customers. Neither chain had a real brand, a signature dish or a trademarked recipe; they competed only on price and on volume of advertising rather than its quality. The company bet everything on "scale itself compounds," and 17% restaurant-level margins in the early 1990s meant nobody dared question the playbook.

9:07 Same-store sales fell for five straight years and nobody knew why
In 1994 same-store sales turned negative and stayed red for five consecutive years; sales were flat for over a decade and lost ground to inflation. Nothing about the restaurants themselves had changed: nearly 40% of both chains' locations had been opened or remodeled in the previous two years, price increases were small, and after the merger there was no competitor left. But the traffic simply stopped coming, as if Americans had suddenly had enough starting in the mid-1990s, and the novelty of the format and the chains faded for no clear reason. The company tried fix after fix, all of them one-year band-aids: in 1995 it cut advertising below 1% of sales to buy profit, and the next year posted the worst same-store sales in its history; only tripling the ad budget turned same-store sales positive — meaning it had to keep marketing and sacrifice margin just to get people through the door.

11:07 Six years under private equity and traffic never improved once
In 2000 a New York private equity firm borrowed more than $500 million to take Buffets Inc. private. The spreadsheet logic was beautiful: cut costs, maximize earnings, cover the acquisition debt's interest with cash flow, squeeze the remaining customers and then re-list. But over the six-year holding period traffic never improved. The firm immediately raised prices, cut staff and service, then compensated with promotions, which only alienated customers further and eroded margin. By 2005 the once-healthy company was stuffed with debt, the firm had taken $90 million in dividends for itself, and what was left was a shell paying lenders more interest than its restaurants earned. Buying Ryan's was just a bigger dose of the same disease — the money came from selling off the land under most of Ryan's restaurants, turning the one asset that didn't depend on traffic into a new annual rent bill.

15:09 No meat was Fresh Choice's profit itself
Fresh Choice tried to solve the economics from the other end: replace expensive protein, which drives up food cost, with cheap salad and carbs. It charged the same prices in Northern California as Old Country and Hometown did in Ohio, yet its food cost stayed 10% below its rivals' — that gap was the entire profit. But customers consistently refused to pay more without a real main course, and every investment meant to justify a price increase only accelerated the churn. The company couldn't give in either, because "no meat" was precisely where its profit came from. It tried uniform pricing, eliminating discounts, adding chicken to the salad, launching thicker soups, designing smaller and cheaper new store formats — none of it worked. By the late 1990s, falling traffic plus a complete lack of pricing power dragged the company into annual losses and penny-stock territory.

21:14 Even the most efficient operator went down all the same
Sweet Tomatoes was the most efficient, most disciplined operator in the industry, and it still came apart. From the start it made itself a destination: standalone restaurants with private parking on land it owned, rather than renting in strip malls like its rivals. Each store had a 55-foot salad bar, eight made-from-scratch soups, a baked potato bar, a dessert bar, a pasta station and a bakery, and from the 1980s it pushed signature items like tuna tarragon and Joan's broccoli madness — branded dishes that injected crucial credibility. For sites it picked business districts and near shopping centers that could capture both lunch and dinner, buying land where it could and otherwise locking in 30-year leases. It also centralized on both ends, prep and stores, building 19 central kitchens to cook in bulk and distribute to each location, and during expansion placing new stores near a central kitchen to keep capacity utilized. But logic and discipline only delayed the inevitable.

24:14 What killed the buffet was the supermarket deli counter
The way the three giants died was no coincidence: Fresh Choice had the cheapest food and died because customers wouldn't pay more than $7 for dinner; Sweet Tomatoes ran the most efficiently and survived as long as it did only because it owned the land under its restaurants; Buffets Inc. had the most locations, the cheapest labor and the strongest economies of scale, and still couldn't raise prices without losing customers. The fast-food and casual chains that had piggybacked on the 1980s drew the conclusion first — by the late 1990s Wendy's, Burger King and KFC had all shut down their salad bars and unlimited bundles, because none of them made money. The real killer came from inside the supermarket: frozen meals failed to disrupt the buffet because they're single-serving while a buffet is designed for families; but dinner simply moved to the deli counter of the same supermarket. A supermarket doesn't need the deli to support the whole store, it prices by the pound and by the piece, customers already come in weekly for milk and eggs, and the deli is a zero-acquisition-cost cross-sell that shares labor and overhead.

30:22 The buffet couldn't pull a single one of the four profit levers
Every restaurant has only four levers to profit: raise prices, shrink portions, cut labor, shrink the footprint. The buffet chains had none of them. They couldn't raise prices, couldn't cut labor, couldn't shrink portions, couldn't shrink the restaurant. Since the 1990s the whole restaurant industry has moved toward "do more in less space," but a buffet can never be truly efficient — it needs those square feet to hold the variety that makes it appealing, and once it goes big it has to stay big. That worked in the 1980s, when land was cheap, malls were sprouting everywhere and landlords cared more about traffic than rent. But as malls fell out of favor, retail migrated and e-commerce hollowed out strip centers, these chains found themselves locked into 10,000-square-foot boxes nobody wanted. That's why every chain filed Chapter 11 over and over — bankruptcy was the only legal way out of hundreds of leases no one would take over.

item.title: More Collaboration Makes You Slower: Counterintuitive Management from the Product Chiefs at Snap and Discord
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-lennys-协作越多越慢-snap-和-discord-产品一号位反直觉管理法/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-lennys-协作越多越慢-snap-和-discord-产品一号位反直觉管理法/
item.description: Collaboration has hidden costs nobody has internalized, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So Peter Sellis deliberately and aggressively internalizes the cost of collaboration, rather than defaulting to more collaboration being better.
item.content:encoded:
Collaboration has hidden costs nobody has internalized, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So Peter Sellis deliberately and aggressively internalizes the cost of collaboration, rather than defaulting to more collaboration being better.

High information density, but the back half is worth more than the front half. For people who want to hear how a product leader actually makes decisions, not for people who want specific growth playbooks.

6:07 The more you collaborate, the slower the system runs
Peter says you will never hear an executive say ‘stop collaborating,’ and to him that is precisely a warning sign. Collaboration brings enormous coordination costs, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So he consciously and aggressively internalizes the cost of collaboration, rather than defaulting to more collaboration being better. This is also where his ‘design teams like a terrorist organization’ comes from: one ideological culture that makes everyone understand why you are doing this thing, plus a very clear organizational structure that specifies who can be trusted to make which decision. With those two things, you don't need to over-collaborate and you still get results that feel ‘as if you had collaborated.’

16:12 The median PM gap is a mathematical structure problem
Peter offers a distributional explanation: product management ability is normally distributed in the population, and the people who actually become PMs are cut from the right tail; once you cut it, it becomes a power-law distribution, and the median of a power-law distribution is far below the mean. Layer on two more mechanisms: in the ZERP era it became the most lucrative career in tech for people without a technical background, and the definition is subjective, so the people who get in have an extremely strong incentive to stay; meanwhile the genuinely strong ones have skills that fit almost perfectly into other executive roles or into founding their own companies, so ‘great product managers are exiting the system.’ Squeezed from both ends, the median is naturally bad. He also points out that the people actually complaining about PMs are the middle cohort of engineers — great engineers know how to bend a PM into the shape they want, and especially bad engineers can hide behind the PM's decisions.

21:16 Snap's ad business can't scale for three mathematical reasons
First, users are extremely young, and between 17 and 18, and between 18 and 21, there is a ‘suspicious discontinuous jump’ in ad CPMs in and outside the US; the rules for tracking, measuring and targeting under-17s are extremely strict, and what is hard to measure is hard to build performance products around. Second, almost all non-search display advertising runs on a screen that shows ads, whereas what Snap opens is a camera — in the core flow of taking a snap and sending it to a friend, there is no logical place to put an ad; it is a creation-oriented product, not a consumption-oriented one. Third, it is fundamentally a messaging app, and there is currently no good messaging ad product; Asian chat apps get cited over and over, but break it down by dollars spent per unit of time and none of them does especially well.

35:25 Taste is the nerve to leave good things on the shelf
Peter says one thing he learned at Snap: he watched Evan say no to better ideas than almost anything any other consumer startup has ever shipped. He describes the product leader's goal as turning the founder into the world's richest museum curator — what is on display in the product at any moment is only a small part of the whole collection, the pieces the curator judges suitable for this time and place. He offers a way to probe taste in an interview: ask the person about something they built but never shipped — not something killed because the data was bad, but something they held in their hands as a prototype and then judged ‘the world isn't ready’ or ‘this thing isn't ready.’ If a museum hung its entire collection on the walls, the curator would have done nothing.

40:29 Advertising is the internet's product-market fit
Peter comes down squarely on Eric Seufert's side: advertising is the internet's product-market fit, and subscription consumer products are overrated. He judges OpenAI to have ‘last mover advantage’ in advertising — Meta already solved the modern ad auction as a ‘solved problem’ from 2010 to 2020, and OpenAI is just running through each component quickly. Mechanically he names the modified VCG (Vickrey-Clarke-Groves) auction: it isn't the highest bidder who wins, but rather the advertiser's natural value for that user is folded into the bid, so whoever bids high has to pay more to reach people who don't want to be reached. This mechanism lets organic content and ad content go into the same auction, with dollars as the common denominator.

42:30 In chat, the denominator for ads is trust, not relevance
Peter replaces ‘natural value’ in VCG with ‘trust’ in the chat context. A user asks ‘which microphone should I buy,’ and the product has to decide whether to give an objective answer, a set of answers, or an advertiser-influenced one — and the degree of influence should equal how much trust you are willing to trade away. He uses Amazon search as an example: search for something and you scroll past 16 ads before seeing the first real result, which subtly erodes users' trust in the system. So OpenAI's real deciding factor isn't whether to do ads, but how to mathematically maximize long-term trust inside the auction mechanism — trust maximization is very likely correlated with user retention, and may even be causal.

50:35 Growth comes from the core, not from new markets
Verified twice at Snap and Discord: a network-effects business wants to grow on its own, and the most effective move is to serve the people already using it, or wanting to use it for its actual job, better — faster, more relevant. He explains with eighth-grade math: it takes 30 monthly actives to equal one daily active, so consumer products should optimize the DAU/MAU ratio; moving that ratio a few basis points is far more worthwhile than pulling in a pile of new MAUs and gambling on retention. Snap's lesson came from the disastrous 2018 redesign, the only quarter-over-quarter time Snap's overall DAU went flat, after which the team ground away at Android performance and produced a multi-year growth revival. Discord's version is more counterintuitive: at the time Midjourney was built on Discord and everyone outside thought this was Discord's big opportunity, but Peter says if you pull up the Discord usage curve, you simply cannot pick out the Midjourney segment.

1:02:44 SpaceX is burning its own ships by hand
Peter considers SpaceX the greatest company right now, and the most worth learning from is how it fights the future: Falcon 9 is the world's best reusable launch system, other countries would trade GDP for it, and yet SpaceX announced it will stop selling Falcon 9 seats in a few years and pivot to Starship. He calls it a Cortez-level burning of the ships, a way to avoid what Christensen called the innovator's dilemma — because even holding the best thing in hand, you are still willing to build the thing that makes your current product irrelevant. He also notes that SpaceX and Tesla publish ten-year plans openly on their websites, and Tesla even open-sources its patents; that confidence — ‘I'll tell you what to do, and if you think you can do it better, come copy it’ — is what he aspires to as a product leader.

item.title: They Tried to Give Hip-Hop's Pioneers Their Money. Some Thought It Was a Scam.
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-a16z-给嘻哈元老发钱-他们以为是诈骗/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-a16z-给嘻哈元老发钱-他们以为是诈骗/
item.description: Some didn't even show up to collect the award, because they didn't believe it was real. Handing cash out directly doesn't work in hip-hop — in Nas's telling, you have to give recognition and dignity first, and only then can the money be accepted.
item.content:encoded:
Some didn't even show up to collect the award, because they didn't believe it was real. Handing cash out directly doesn't work in hip-hop — in Nas's telling, you have to give recognition and dignity first, and only then can the money be accepted.

This isn't an investment interview; it's a roundtable on how to pay back a debt owed to a culture. Worth hearing if you care about distribution mechanisms in the creator economy, or if you want to know what Ben Horowitz has been quietly working on.

2:04 A $10 album owed $5 million back
The starting point is a debt Ben Horowitz owed himself: he bought the album Paid in Full for $10, and over his career he extracted at least $5 million in value from that record, with no channel to pay any of it back — and he felt he had to. He called Steve Stoute first, who said the idea wasn't just good but overdue: everyone was saying these old rappers were broke and dusty, but nobody was actually doing anything. The second call went to Nas, who said Quincy Jones's Jazz Foundation model wouldn't work in hip-hop: you can't just give a person money, it has to be recognition of what he did and who he is, and it has to be more than money. So the form became an awards show and a Grandmaster Award, with Scarface and Rakim in the first class of honorees.

5:05 Some thought it was a scam and skipped the award
The foundation's first obstacle wasn't money, it was disbelief. Ben says the early level of distrust was beyond what you'd imagine, and for a while they struggled to actually get money into people's hands — some didn't even come to accept the award because they thought it was a scam, and others said, "I don't need anyone giving me money." He treats that disbelief as evidence the design was right: it can't look like reparations, it has to be a celebration and a tribute, shining the light they're owed on them, and only then will it be accepted. Caz later put it more bluntly: the industry has shortchanged these people for so long that the first reaction can only be, "Why is anyone helping us now?"

10:07 The first hip-hop hit was stolen from him
Grandmaster Caz wrote the rhyme that became Rapper's Delight, his own name is even in the rhyme, and the first hip-hop hit was taken out of his hands just like that, with nothing coming back to him. Ben says everyone in the music industry knew about it, but nobody ever did anything, and nobody ever said anything. The first time he met Caz in New York he was stunned: this is a man who changes the energy of any room he walks into today, carries no bitterness at all, and still thinks of himself as a star. Steve added: it's not that nobody knew — not enough people knew. The industry knew; the public didn't.

17:10 Dr. Dre needed an introduction to meet his idols
Steve Stoute tells a detail: Dr. Dre heard about Paid in Full and decided to come, then asked whether Steve could introduce him to Kool Moe Dee — Dre had never met him. Another time, in Las Vegas, Dre asked whether he could be introduced to Slick Rick, whom he had also never met. A Dre who has made it has to ask for an introduction to meet these legends, which shows how fragmented the scene is — and getting these people into one room only happened because of this foundation. Caz puts it more directly: the industry separates people by success, status and who's hot, and for years his meetings with Nas were chance encounters; now they see each other once a year and can just call.

32:20 The Grammys botched it, so they did it themselves
Quincy Jones was the legend of legends to this group, but when he died, the Grammy tribute was called out flatly as botched. The Quincy Jones Award wasn't conceived to fill a slot — it came from seeing the Grammys get it wrong, and Quincy's son QD3 saying they'd do it themselves, which is how it became a fixed annual award from the foundation. This year's recipient is Nile Rodgers. Steve mentions that George Clinton showed up last year with his "mothership" prop and, at 83, recited the lyrics to Rakim's Follow the Leader on stage — a man who changed music, paying tribute to another man who changed music.

39:24 Hip-hop has no social security
Caz explained what the money actually means: it's a grant paid out over five years, and he bought a house and moved out of the projects. He lived in the Bronx his whole life, and for the past ten to fifteen years his last thought at night was always, "I don't want to die in the projects"; now he and his wife live in a house in Pennsylvania. He says hip-hop has no social security and no health insurance, you have to keep working, which is why you still see him doing radio, playing parks and running hip-hop tours — because he has to. The money gave him something he'd never had: a buffer. He also made a point of saying money is only part of it; the real thing is being put in the light.

44:26 Brands came back from the dead on hip-hop
Steve Stoute uses business data to argue why the debt is legitimate: Adidas had only a 2% market share in the US at the time, three-quarters of it from the Northeast, and the company just saw a group of people buying the same shoe obsessively and throwing the laces away, with no idea why. Grand Puba's line "First things first, obey your thirst" later became Sprite's ad slogan. Tommy Hilfiger was selling ties that wouldn't move, drove through Harlem, saw everyone wearing their pants low with the Calvin Klein waistband showing, went back and made the underwear waistband wider and thicker with his own name on it, and only then did the brand take off. These brands exist because of what these people contributed.

48:31 Love isn't writing a check, it's flying to Houston
Ben tells a story about his wife, Felicia, who is also the foundation's chair, to show how this organization differs from other philanthropy: Scarface had a heart condition and needed open-heart surgery, but he came from a place where people barely even go to the doctor, he was scared, and on the phone he said he wasn't going. Felicia flew to Houston and said no, you're going now. Just as they walked into the exam room, his aorta ruptured, and the doctors got him in in time and saved his life. Steve adds the everyday version: she'll call out of the blue to ask how you and your family are doing, and if someone in your family gets sick, flowers show up the next day, or whatever was agreed shows up.

item.title: Fashion Mogul: Stop Apologizing for Being a Working Mom, and Talk About Money
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-wsjournal-时尚大亨-当妈不必道歉-钱要开口谈/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-wsjournal-时尚大亨-当妈不必道歉-钱要开口谈/
item.description: Emma Grede says if women avoid talking about money, money avoids them; by talking about it first, picking the right partners, and doing the business others can't be bothered with, she turned overlooked customers into loyal repeat buyers.
item.content:encoded:
Emma Grede says if women avoid talking about money, money avoids them; by talking about it first, picking the right partners, and doing the business others can't be bothered with, she turned overlooked customers into loyal repeat buyers.

Medium information density. The first half is about brands and partnerships; the second half, on money mindset and maternal guilt, is the more valuable part. Good for a commute.

3:18 A celebrity is an accelerator, not a partner
Grede says that if you throw a star and a brand together expecting to make money or build credibility, you will quickly find it doesn't hold up. A star buys you one burst of exposure and attention, but it doesn't keep customers; only a strong loyalty to a good product brings people back. That's why she insists on treating the Kardashian sisters as real business partners rather than spokespeople — the partnership has to be bigger than ‘how many followers someone has’. She admits she was lucky to find partners capable of doing that.

4:19 Target the market nobody is taking seriously
Grede says that before any business she looks at the competitive landscape first, and knows clearly what is declining and what might be needed. When Good American entered the plus-size market in 2016, the whole industry treated it as a ‘bonus 15%’ add-on, and even today's talking points didn't exist. She believes it was rewriting the rules completely in a space where nobody was innovating and customers weren't understood that made the company work. She stresses that she never watches fashion week and never chases trends, because ‘if you're led by trends, you'll die very quickly’.

7:28 The harder the business, the more it's worth doing
On Off Season sportswear, Grede says women are badly overlooked in fan merchandise: the stands are full of women, and women hold the household's purchasing decisions, yet all they can buy is generic hoodies and oversized T-shirts. She sees that as a huge business opportunity. She also admits that negotiating licenses with the NFL, NBA and WNBA ‘isn't a question of spending money, it's extremely hard to do’ — but what excites her is precisely doing things that require huge investment and can bring huge returns, provided you really understand where the opportunity is and don't cut corners.

10:31 If you don't talk about money, money avoids you
Grede says that managing hundreds of employees and sitting on several company boards, she has observed a pattern at work: avoid conversations about money and money will avoid you. Men talk about money anywhere, anytime — mortgages, credit card rates, investment opportunities, big and small; women lack enough of those conversations, and enough specifics. She believes the money stories we hear growing up stay with us unless someone tells us something different. That's why she does a podcast and wrote a book: to break that silence rather than hoard the information.

13:46 What she cares about is the path to ownership
Asked about her net worth, Grede says the figure Forbes reported ‘missed a little’, but her favorite line is ‘who cares about those valuations’. What she really cares about is the path to ownership: as a school leaver with very little education and someone who only came to America less than a decade ago, by any normal logic those numbers shouldn't belong to her. She deliberately and consciously put herself in that position, took on a lot of risk, and made a lot of trade-offs. She also pushes back on the idea that you can manifest your way to millions, saying that doesn't work.

15:48 Mom guilt is a story handed down to us
Grede says that guilt is a story passed down through generations of grandmothers and mothers, with a default logic: if you're in New York and away from your kids, you should feel enormous guilt. But she says she actually enjoys it — three nights in a hotel, sleeping diagonally across the whole bed. She thinks many women actually feel fine about being away from their kids for a few days, it's just not cool to say so. She acknowledges she has childcare, infrastructure and a good partner, so she isn't permanently in apology mode about it, and says she has cleared that behavior out of her thoughts and her vocabulary.

17:49 A three-hour mom at most — a joke, and also true
Grede explains her ‘three-hour mom at most’ line: she works Monday to Friday, and not nine to five, so by Saturday she isn't going to sit with her kids all day or make the whole weekend revolve around them — by noon she's ‘had enough of you lot’. She says it's a joke, but it's also saying: you're allowed to be honest about parenting differently, and different doesn't mean you're a good or bad mom. She thinks the better question is ‘what don't you do, and where do you spend your time’, which is more useful to any woman.

19:50 Women keep putting the rules on trial themselves
Asked how she differs from Lean In or Girlboss, Grede says she doesn't think she's offering anything new, she's just telling her own truth, and she has the chance to tell it more fully than a 30-second video. She thinks the topic lingers in pop culture because we can't accept it — the rules set for women are constantly judged, discussed and argued over by women ourselves, and some of the responsibility for that is ours. She says every man in the room probably has no idea what she's talking about and just thinks ‘so what, carry on’. She argues for accepting that our ways differ while the goal is shared: more women in power is a good thing.

item.title: Does the Early Bird Really Catch the Worm? Or Could the Night Owl Get There First?
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-nostupid-早起的鸟有虫吃-晚睡的鼠有奶酪/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-nostupid-早起的鸟有虫吃-晚睡的鼠有奶酪/
item.description: Early risers earning more is only a correlation — you can't tell whether the social structure favours early risers or whether early risers are simply different people; and chronotype is biological, not a choice of willpower.
item.content:encoded:
Early risers earning more is only a correlation — you can't tell whether the social structure favours early risers or whether early risers are simply different people; and chronotype is biological, not a choice of willpower.

Medium information density, but it delivers two judgment-changing points — that chronotype is biological rather than a matter of willpower, and that early risers earning more is only a correlation — plus one actionable light-dimming method.

3:07 Chronotype is biological, not a choice of willpower
Angela and Stephen discuss the concept of chronotype — whether a person naturally becomes alert in the morning or the evening. Angela calls herself a lark, often waking before the alarm goes off. Stephen stresses that the 2017 Nobel Prize in Medicine went to circadian rhythm research, which shows this is biological — even plants have biological clocks, because the Earth rotates on its axis, there is day and there is night, and organisms must predict and adapt to that rotation. So the answer to "why don't you just be a morning person" is that this trait is extremely hardwired.

8:12 Teenagers sleeping late has biological evidence, it isn't laziness
Angela cites a 2017 PLOS ONE paper that used 12 years of diary data from the American Time Use Survey and found that chronotype is near-normally distributed both overall and within every age group, with the mean shifting systematically with age: later through adolescence, peaking at its latest around age 19, then shifting earlier. In other words, teenagers' bodies tending toward late sleep has evidentiary support. The paper also found that before age 40 men generally have later chronotypes than women, and after 40 it reverses. This supports the recommendation to push back school start times.

9:17 Later school start times have measurable benefits
In 2017 the Seattle school district pushed middle and high school start times from 7:50 to 8:45, nearly an hour later. Researchers from the University of Washington and the Salk Institute used this to measure sleep-wake cycles and found students' median sleep duration increased by 34 minutes, with measurable benefits. The RAND think tank, building on these studies, estimated that delaying middle and high school start times alone would yield $8.6 billion in economic productivity gains. This shows sleep schedule is not an individual problem but a system design problem.

11:23 Early risers earn more, but it's only a correlation
Danish economist Jens Banke published a 2012 paper, "Do Morning-type People Earn More Than Evening-type People? How Chronotypes Influence Income," whose analysis showed morning types earn significantly more than evening types, and that being a morning person benefits men in particular. But Stephen stresses this is correlational data and cannot be called causal. Being a morning person correlates not only with income but also with happiness, productivity and health. So you cannot distinguish: whether morning people are simply more productive people (a spurious correlation), or whether the social structure favours morning people.

13:26 COVID was a forced experiment, and people generally pushed back their wake times
Stephen says one thing learned from COVID is that many people are able to and prefer to work in very different ways. Angela adds that a big silver lining of COVID was a forced experiment, and research shows people really did change their sleep patterns: when they didn't have to be in the office at 9 and had more flexibility, people generally shifted their wake times later, more like weekends than weekdays. This proves the rigid nine-to-five system is not immutable — it's just that before 2020 no one was forced to test it.

20:00 The email signature solves an empathy problem, not an efficiency problem
Stephen says he's a morning person and often sends work emails at 5 a.m.; he thinks email doesn't demand an instant reply, so it's fine. But some people who receive early-morning emails think, "He sent it at 5, I only woke up at 7, I have to reply right away." So Angela added a line to the end of every email: "my work hours may not be your work hours, reply if you want, when you want." She says it's a tribute to her late friend Seagal Barsade, a scientist who studied emotion and empathy. Barsade was a famous night owl who wrote on every email, "my work hours may not be your work hours, please don't feel obligated to reply outside normal working hours."

24:05 The most effective lever for shifting your schedule is controlling light
Angela learned from Stanford neuroscientist Andrew Huberman's podcast that you can adjust your natural circadian rhythm by controlling light. Huberman recommends getting daylight within 15 minutes of waking, especially important in the low-sunlight winter months. Angela moved her laptop from her basement office to an upstairs spot by a window. Huberman also recommends minimising light later in the day, i.e. dimming the lights at home after dark. Angela says she's also more careful about not playing on her phone, and instead reads on an old black-and-white-only Kindle, which she finds helps.

27:18 From early bird to night owl is the biological clock shifting with age
At 17, Angela wrote a college application essay titled "Confessions of a Teenage Owl," in which she called sleep a "needless waste of time," said she slept only four hours a night, and claimed she was "just as healthy and twice as happy for it." Stephen says anyone in medicine or science today would want to delete that sentence. Angela is now 52, says she tries to sleep more, and likens herself to "the wise owl is to the early morning lark" — she went from early bird to night owl. This confirms the paper's finding that chronotype shifts with age.

item.title: There's a pain axis inside the model, and it only lights up when the model itself is involved
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-19-cogrev-模型里有一条痛觉轴-只在涉及自身时激活/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-19-cogrev-模型里有一条痛觉轴-只在涉及自身时激活/
