Ali gives this curve: in 2018 and 2019, a CVE took roughly two to three years from disclosure to weaponization; by 2022 it was down to eight or nine months; from 2022 to now it has compressed to essentially hours, almost no time at all. The reason is that data and AI are merging with the cybersecurity market — companies run large numbers of agents internally, generating massive logs and traces, and the volume of data that needs analyzing is orders of magnitude larger than a year or two ago.

32:44 Say AI will destroy the world, then ask if you want IPO allocation
Ali concedes two things can be true at once: some people really are scared by AI risk, and some people want regulation to "pace us" — because slowing down benefits them. People can always reconcile self-interest and fear into a harmonious whole in their heads, he says. The industry has long had this marketing play: the moment a new model is trained, shout about how terrifyingly good it is, and the world's attention arrives. But he also gives the other side: the time from CVE to actual weaponized exploit went from years to minutes in three or four years, and cyberattacks are real. So "scary" is both a genuine risk and excellent marketing.

39:50 Enterprises have no agents, only faster search
Ali polled the room live: he asked how many in the audience were managing hundreds or thousands of agents coordinating and negotiating with each other, and almost no hands went up. What most enterprises use is Microsoft Copilot, essentially a chatbot — "a very, very glorified, efficient Google search." Coding is the only scenario that has truly landed, and even there the ROI is debatable. He thinks the reason isn't that models aren't smart enough, but that models lack the organization's internal context: they haven't sat in every meeting, don't know what's in everyone's head, don't know the processes. Every organization has a few employees who know everything, and when you tap them on the shoulder you think, "what if he quits?" Pour that context into today's frontier models and you get enormous productivity — and that doesn't require a smarter model.

47:01 Ontology is that employee who's been there five years
Ali explains ontology with a concrete picture: two people equally smart, equally hardworking, with identical educational backgrounds — one on their first day, one who's been there five years. The difference is that the latter knows how the organization runs, who people are, how things get done — "don't look at the org chart, don't ask that guy, he can't get anything done." That is ontology: tacit knowledge scattered across everyone's heads. He contrasts it with the state of agents today: the agentic loop looks up resources one at a time, like Google crawling ten sites live on every search, taking ten minutes, and then handing you ten blue links — expensive, slow and bad. Google's answer was the index, and AI also needs that index computed offline, only harder — because of permission constraints, since data I can access isn't necessarily data you can access, and the object types go far beyond web pages.

56:08 Same model, different harness, twice the cost
Databricks' answer is a full cost-governance stack: Unity Gateway provides token capacity for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Grok and open-source models, sets budget caps and alerts by person and by group, does cost forecasting analytics, and adds intelligent routing to switch to cheaper models when nearing budget or when the question is simple. Ali gives a concrete number: the same model, the same version, just a different harness, and actual cost can differ by nearly 2x. Their in-house harness is called Omnigent, which can multiplex across different harnesses. The result is token usage keeps climbing while AI cost stays roughly flat.

item.title: AI demand still runs ahead of supply, but the compute bottleneck is turning into a political problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-mastersinbiz-ai-需求仍跑在供给前面-但算力瓶颈正在变成政治问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-mastersinbiz-ai-需求仍跑在供给前面-但算力瓶颈正在变成政治问题/
item.description: Light Street's Glen Kacher sees AI as a 15-to-20-year rebuild of the computing stack, and says only the first third of the first stage is done; the real risk is not over-investing in CapEx but power and local politics slowing construction.
item.content:encoded:
Light Street's Glen Kacher sees AI as a 15-to-20-year rebuild of the computing stack, and says only the first third of the first stage is done; the real risk is not over-investing in CapEx but power and local politics slowing construction.

An investor running a tech hedge fund in the heart of Silicon Valley strings AI compute, semiconductors, open-source models and the power bottleneck into one investable chain of judgment, at high information density.

7:16 Buy only the best company, never the second or third
Over 13 years at Integral Capital, Kacher made 46 private investments, and the lesson he drew is: do not buy the second- or third-best company in an industry, always buy the best one you can get. The reason is that in tech the leader takes two-thirds of the market, the number two gets 20% to 25% at most, and everyone else fights over scraps. Higher margins plus a dominant share compound the lead. But he also concedes that incumbents in tech get disrupted, and disruption usually comes not from big companies but from small ones — AI and the semiconductors behind AI are exactly the test case for that rule.

8:17 Nvidia's moat is underrated
Kacher says many people assume Nvidia will lose its roughly 85% share of the AI accelerator market, and the shift to inference does give competitors an opening. But he thinks the market currently underrates Nvidia's own capacity to innovate. He describes the evolution of inference chips as an alphabet progression from CPU to FPU to GPU to XPU, where X stands for the unknown: Google has TPU, there are options like Trainium, and Nvidia itself bought the Grok inference line. He judges that inference will ultimately be a bigger market than training, so there will be many chip forms and many opportunities to innovate.

21:51 Four semiconductor companies are 40% of the portfolio
TSMC, Nvidia, Broadcom and AMD make up roughly 40% of Light Street's public holdings, a highly concentrated portfolio. Kacher's logic: concentrate capital where innovation is densest, and right now the densest place is the core of AI accelerated computing. Nvidia has more than 80% of the GPU networking market and AMD is catching up; as agentic AI becomes the next growth driver, AMD has a unique edge because it is one of the two big players in both desktop and server CPUs; Broadcom has built TPUs for Google for years and now has opportunities with big players like OpenAI; TSMC fabs for all three, so it wins no matter who wins, an almost oligopolistic or even monopolistic position.

26:01 Open-source models are fighting a price war
Kacher thinks the battle between Anthropic and OpenAI is happening in real time, and that Google remains a player thanks to Gemini and its search distribution advantage, so it cannot be ruled out. But the battlefield that is really emerging is open-source models: they are free, can be downloaded to run on local hardware, or run on someone else's commoditized hardware in the cloud, competing directly with the two big companies' expensive frontier models. He judges that early signals show both approaches have their place. At the same time he points to the regulatory problem: open-source models can be put inside your own software and tuned to your needs, and regulators actually have few options, because these models are already out in the wild.

33:14 Someone was saying GPUs should do AI back in 2005
Kacher recalls that while at Integral, Kleiner Perkins partner Bill Joy mentioned a group of engineers at Caltech using GPUs for early AI computation, around 2005 or 2006, and Bill Joy's conclusion was that GPUs would be the chip architecture best suited to AI computation. It stayed in his head. Later, on every visit to Nvidia, Jensen would talk about AI, but at the time AI was only a tiny end market for Nvidia, and crypto mattered far more. In the second half of 2022 the crypto crash and the takeoff of AI happened at the same time, the market was more focused on crypto and pushed the stock down, which in turn gave them the chance to build a position in Nvidia.

45:36 The giants are not over-investing, they are catching up
Faced with the challenge that AI could be over-provisioned like fiber, Kacher's answer is: Amazon, Microsoft and Google are building the compute stack in partnership with Anthropic and OpenAI, and the question is how far ahead of demand they plan. His judgment is that today they are not ahead, they are behind and catching up. Bears expect them to over-invest, but that has not happened today. He concedes there are real bottlenecks, including the memory companies and TSMC, which cannot invest as fast as they would like, so today demand still runs far ahead of supply, and the pessimism around AI is misplaced.

52:47 A fifteen-year cycle, and only a third is done
Kacher likens AI to the shift from client-server to internet architecture, a computing cycle that happens roughly every 15 to 25 years. The old technology was a search-then-retrieve model, with data sitting in databases; AI generates a custom answer for your question and your data on every use, and is far more compute-intensive. The rhythm he gives: infrastructure development takes about 5 to 10 years, years 6 to 16 are when the platform or operating system takes shape, and years 11 to 21 are when applications become the main venue for enterprise investment and innovation. By that framework, roughly a third of the first stage is done today, and the whole cycle is at least 15 to 20 years.

53:48 Power and local politics have become the new bottleneck
Kacher treats political resistance to data centers as a real risk: any bottleneck that slows technology adoption is a problem. He says it is not yet a big problem today, but it is an emerging one. His solution is that the industry has to explain itself proactively: Northern Virginia, as the data center capital of the world, has brought the area tax revenue and blue-collar demand for electricians, plumbers and construction workers, a shot in the arm for the economy. He mentions a data center project in San Mateo that plans to put Bloom Energy natural gas fuel cells behind the meter, with almost no emissions and almost no noise, and residents still opposed it because they had "heard data centers are bad." He sees this as an education problem, requiring energy, jobs and tax revenue to be explained project by project, from local to national.

item.title: The Pizza Tracker: We Were Trained to Pay for Fake Progress Bars
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-planetmoney-披萨追踪器-我们被驯化成愿意为假进度条买单/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-planetmoney-披萨追踪器-我们被驯化成愿意为假进度条买单/
item.description: Domino's pizza tracker started as an internal management tool and became a global app standard. It works because it turns waiting into visible work; and once companies discovered we love watching progress bars, they started faking them.
item.content:encoded:
Domino's pizza tracker started as an internal management tool and became a global app standard. It works because it turns waiting into visible work; and once companies discovered we love watching progress bars, they started faking them.

Medium information density, but the second half on "deliberate slowdowns" and "fake progress bars" is worth the price. Suited to listeners interested in product design and consumer psychology.

2:07 The 30-minute guarantee sold control, not speed
Domino's once promised delivery in 30 minutes or it was free. The guarantee made drivers speed, caused deaths and lawsuits, and was eventually dropped. But David Halbenstricker has a theory: the guarantee was popular not just because it was fast, but because it gave customers a sense of control. In the early 2000s Domino's commissioned a study and found that the customer's psychology after ordering a pizza is a roller coaster: the peak is at the moment of ordering, then it slides all the way down — "Where's my pizza? Did they lose my order?" No matter how long the actual wait, what customers hate is the waiting itself.

8:16 The internal tool had to work before customers got one
Executives did not initially want to build a pizza tracker, because tracking every pizza at every store was too time-consuming and looked like a gimmick. What they were really obsessed with was "out-the-door time." A UK franchisee put the out-the-door times of five to ten nearby stores on a single display so they would compete with each other, and paid cash bonuses to the top-ranked stores. After David's boss visited the UK, he had David replicate the system in the US. David connected each store's out-the-door time to a central system and built a real-time dashboard. The CEO said it was the thing that most drove performance during his tenure.

11:25 The tracker was a byproduct of the internal system
David and a colleague realized they already had a system tracking every pizza, so they decided to "hitch a ride" and build a customer-facing tracker. In 2006 most people didn't have smartphones; FedEx, UPS and Amazon could track packages, but on a timescale of days, not minutes. Real-time tracking of pizza progress was entirely new. The designer's interface looked like a horizontal thermometer: order, prep, bake, box, delivery — each completed step turned the next segment red. When David saw the mockup he said: "That's a hot dog. We're a pizza company, why is there a hot dog?" But executives liked it, and decided to launch before the Super Bowl.

15:36 Designers use the pizza tracker as a meeting prop
Shuya Gong was a design director at IDEO and later taught design at Harvard. Consulting for many companies in the mid-2010s, she found one of the most effective ways to open a meeting was to order a pizza on the spot, project the tracker on the big screen, and ask the client: "How do you feel right now?" She says you can feel the anxiety rise or fall in your body very directly, feel the reassurance and groundedness. Then you can ask: which of those parts do you want your users to feel when they use your product? The pizza tracker became shorthand in her design circle: whenever a client involved waiting, she'd say "they need a pizza tracker."

17:39 The tracker manufactures a "labor illusion"
Shuya says one reason the pizza tracker is popular is that as shopping experiences become more digital, the tracker replicates something important from the physical world — watching other people work. Online experiences lack that visibility, so people get impatient more easily. Researchers found that reminding customers there is labor behind a product makes them value it more, and they called it the "labor illusion." Shuya also describes a stranger mechanism: the tracker changes our perception of time. Like walking somewhere and finding the return trip feels shorter because the route is familiar and has landmarks. The pizza tracker gives us a familiar route and landmarks — pizza being made, on the road, out for delivery — making the wait feel shorter.

19:47 Banks deliberately slow transfers to fake a wait
Working with banks and fintech companies in the mid-2010s, Shuya found their problem was the opposite of Domino's: customers weren't used to transfers being so fast. Two computers talk, confirm the amount, and the money is gone — no road to cross, no cheese to melt. But for people used to money taking a while to arrive, instant arrival "feels suspicious." So companies deliberately slow down the "money tracker," withholding real-time feedback and adding a buffer that makes you wait. Shuya says this is intentionally slowing down time, adding meaningful friction so that in the waiting you feel the seriousness and weight of the transfer. The host presses: isn't that advising lying to customers? Shuya says she prefers to understand it as "curating the experience," adding back the physicality that existed in the traditional experience, to make people comfortable.

21:48 TurboTax and Uber progress bars may be fake
TurboTax pops up an animation during filing that says "we're checking your deductions and credits." But a few years ago someone looked at the code and found the animation is identical for everyone, in every situation, and takes the same amount of time. The question is: is TurboTax trying to reassure us during the terrifying ordeal of filing taxes, or using the labor illusion to make us feel a large payment is worth it? Uber is similar: the host repeatedly got updated pickup times, but the car almost always arrived later than promised. It felt like the tracker was part of a deliberate deception — to make you choose Uber over Lyft, to keep you from cancelling, to get you standing on the street early. The show reached out to TurboTax and Uber; TurboTax did not respond, Uber did not arrange an interview but shared some data suggesting their pickup times are fairly accurate.

25:52 Field test: the pizza tracker is mostly real
Nick biked to a local Domino's to stake it out, while Alex ordered a half-Hawaiian, half-pepperoni pizza at home and monitored the tracker in real time. Nick ordered a pepperoni pizza inside as cover. The tracker showed "Ivan" making the pizza, but when Nick asked the staff their name, they said "Alex." The tracker also showed a "quality check," but Nick saw no quality inspector. David had explained, though, that because Domino's uses conveyor ovens, the bake time is nearly fixed, so the tracker automatically jumps to the next step after a set time. Eventually the pizza came out, was boxed, and was driven off by Alex (aka Ivan), with Nick chasing on his bike and nearly being taken for a stalker. Alex hit "delivered" at Nick's door and the tracker updated quickly. Conclusion: the tracker is mostly accurate, but "Ivan is making it" and the "quality check" are fake.

item.title: AI Proves in Half an Hour a Math Theorem Humans Couldn't Crack in a Year
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-instituteforad-ai-半小时证出人类一年没做出的数学定理/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-instituteforad-ai-半小时证出人类一年没做出的数学定理/
item.description: A stuck L^p problem, and AI produces a five-page proof in half an hour, compressing a 60-page paper down to its core lemma and pushing the threshold for continuous density from 588 to 9.
item.content:encoded:
A stuck L^p problem, and AI produces a five-page proof in half an hour, compressing a 60-page paper down to its core lemma and pushing the threshold for continuous density from 588 to 9.

If you care about what AI can actually do in pure mathematics, this episode gives a case concrete enough to verify: not assisted computation, but a proof structure a human didn't think of.

0:18 For the first time, AI had a good idea
The speaker says this is the first time he has encountered a model that "really had a good idea" on a problem he has worked on for a long time, and that the idea led to "very elegant efficient progress." Note his wording: it isn't that AI did the computation for him, it's that AI produced a proof approach he hadn't thought of. He credits the result to Astra, and says it was done only last week.

8:13 The key theorem: absolute continuity automatically carries L^p
The core theorem is: if a self-similar measure μ is absolutely continuous, then its density automatically lies in some L^p with p greater than 1. What actually excites the speaker isn't the fact itself but that p is quantitative — p can be expressed explicitly in terms of the mass μ gives to small balls. Because p is quantitative, one can bring over the methods used to study explicit absolute continuity, construct explicit L^p examples, and from there get to continuous density.

12:27 p can never be made uniform
The speaker specifically warns: p can never be made uniform. For any dimension d and any p greater than 1, there exists some self-similar measure that lies in L^1 but not in L^p. So this quantitative result must not be read as "all absolutely continuous self-similar measures have uniform L^p integrability" — it is a case-by-case bound that depends on the mass distribution.

23:45 Splitting λ into odd and even parts
The trick for proving continuous density: split the random series of the Bernoulli convolution into odd and even terms; after factoring a λ out of the odd part, what remains is exactly the even part. So μ_λ equals the convolution of μ_{λ²} with itself. If λ² falls in the range where Solomyak proved L^2 holds almost surely, then the convolution of two L^2 functions is continuous, and μ_λ has a continuous density. This is the bridge from an L^2 result to continuity.

34:17 A 60-page paper compressed to 5 pages
The speaker says the core idea was in fact already his and his collaborator's, but that AI was "extremely elegant and efficient" in using it. Varju's paper is 60 pages, his own paper is also very long, and AI compressed the step from one result to another down to 5 pages; and after "maybe a bit of a weakening," another 5 pages gets a stronger conclusion. He stresses this is not AI thinking up the core idea for him, it's AI combining known tools in a way he "could have never" done.

36:18 Half an hour to run, 50 hours to formalise
Asked about runtime, the speaker says "not long, maybe half an hour." The whole result was then formalised in Lean, which took about 50 hours. He also mentions tricks like a goal command that let the model "really try hard." The comparison: he himself might have taken a year, and "if you sent me this paper to referee, I would like who is this person?"

39:21 The continuous-density threshold moves from 588 to 9
For the case λ = 1 - 1/n, AI proves μ_λ is continuous when n is greater than 588 — the speaker says this is not yet the result of him pushing the constant, and "if I push the constant, I could easily push the constant more." Even more striking is another result: absolutely continuous when n is greater than 9, which the speaker says "I could not dare think I could prove"; he himself pushed for two and a half hours to get to 9, while the ideal target is 3.

43:23 The key lemma comes from an obscure paper
At the heart of the proof is a lemma from geometric measure theory: for an L^1 positive function f, if the mass of a set inside a small ball is small and the integral of f over that set is also small, then f lies in some explicit L^p, with p given explicitly by C, ε, A. The speaker says the lemma is "not too difficult to prove," about a page, but "extremely difficult to find because it's not a very well-known fact" — it was dug out of some random papers.

item.title: Looney Tunes Animator: Characters Aren't Drawn, They're Thought Up
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freshair-乐一通-动画师-角色不是画出来的-是想出来的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freshair-乐一通-动画师-角色不是画出来的-是想出来的/
item.description: Chuck Jones said the key to animation isn't what a character looks like or how it's drawn, but "who he is" — he understood the character first, which let Daffy be cowardly and swaggering at once, and let Bugs Bunny strike back only after being provoked.
item.content:encoded:
Chuck Jones said the key to animation isn't what a character looks like or how it's drawn, but "who he is" — he understood the character first, which let Daffy be cowardly and swaggering at once, and let Bugs Bunny strike back only after being provoked.

The first half, the Chuck Jones interview, is information-dense; the second half, the Cassandra Wilson segment, is mostly music appreciation, so you can listen to just the interview portion.

0:00 Bugs Bunny's violence wouldn't pass review today
Comedian Dustin Nickerson tried showing classic cartoons to his young daughter and found they hadn't become harmless with time: many characters have speech impediments and behave aggressively. Pepe Le Pew forcibly holds a female character so she can't leave, while other characters murder each other — the coyote wants to kill the bird. This runs counter to the cartoon impression in viewers' memories that "everyone is friends."

4:04 A film shelved by Warner was saved by an independent distributor
After Coyote vs. Acme was finished, it was shelved by Warner Bros. Discovery and written off financially. This year an independent distributor bought the rights for $50 million, and last month it finally opened. The film screened in relatively few theaters across the U.S., but it has already recouped almost its entire cost domestically, with another $30 million overseas. The movie itself is about the coyote suing the Acme company, inspired by Ian Frazier's 1990 New Yorker parody article.

7:07 Daffy is cowardly and swaggering at the same time
Chuck Jones said Daffy is funny because he rushes in and fears to take a step at the same time, is both obsequious and domineering — like when we go into the boss's office to ask for a raise, swaggering at the door but obsequious once inside, and with Daffy both happen simultaneously. He admitted he couldn't understand "crazy" characters, so he always had to "pasteurize" a character and figure out who he is. He stressed that the point of character animation isn't what the character looks like, nor how it's drawn, but "who he is."

9:11 Bugs Bunny is a comedy hero, not a comedy loser
Jones first did Duck Amuck with Daffy, then later did Rabbit Rampage with Bugs Bunny, and the same setup didn't hold, because Bugs Bunny isn't that kind of character. He classified Bugs Bunny as a comedy hero, whereas the lineage of comedians like Chaplin and Buster Keaton are half-losers, more like ordinary people. He liked Daffy because Daffy keeps going forward, to the point where he himself would stop for fear of what others would think.

10:14 A two-hour "yes session" where no negative opinions were allowed
After 1946, Warner's cartoons were directed by three people: Fritz Freeling, Bob McKimpson and Jones. Whoever had an idea for a film would call the other directors and writers into a meeting they called a "yes session": for two hours no one was allowed to say anything negative, and if you had nothing to contribute you shut up. The result was that everyone participated in everyone else's films, but each director had absolute control over the content of his own films, and there was no infighting. Jones also admitted that if a good gag he'd given was used by Freeling and the audience laughed, he naturally wanted to go throw up — that's human nature, and it was the Daffy in him.

13:25 The narrower the rules, the better the comedy
Jones believed that in comedy, the more you narrow and restrict a character, the better it works: once Chaplin put on the Little Tramp outfit, what he could do was locked down. Once Roadrunner and Coyote were set in the American Southwest desert, the rules followed — Roadrunner must stay on the road, can never harm Coyote, and Coyote can only harm himself by buying those unlucky Acme products, and apart from "beep-beep" you hear no other sound in the whole film. Bugs Bunny is too strong and easily becomes a bully, so every film first lets him live his own life in his natural rabbit environment, until someone comes to take his skin or his life, and only then does he strike back.

16:30 Hiding one dirty frame in a twenty-fourth of a second
Jones admitted that Warner's animators all drew that kind of pornographic cartoon privately. He himself would sometimes slip a single frame — a twenty-fourth of a second — of a dirty image into a Pepe Le Pew film, then call the office manager over and say there seemed to be a little glitch here that he couldn't figure out. He knew no one could see it, but the manager would be shocked on the spot. He always kept a replacement frame on hand just in case, but he enjoyed doing it, in his words, to "reduce him to moccasins."

17:31 The networks cut films until they were incomprehensible
Jones said his scenes and lines were never censored; that was left to the "brilliant people" at the networks, and what they cut made the whole film incomprehensible. Both CBS and ABC did it. He found it absurd that the Roadrunner series, which drew the most complaints about violence, actually had no violence — Roadrunner never harmed Coyote, and Coyote was simply the victim of his own incompetence.

item.title: The last IMO problem AI could not solve, and its value is not in the answer
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-karpathy-ai-解不出的最后一道-imo-题-价值不在答案/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-karpathy-ai-解不出的最后一道-imo-题-价值不在答案/
item.description: In 2025, fewer than 1% of IMO contestants got full marks on Problem 6, and every AI got stuck on it. What makes it hard is not computation — it is that you must first understand, first have taste, before you start writing. And that is exactly what reinforcement learning struggles most to train.
item.content:encoded:
In 2025, fewer than 1% of IMO contestants got full marks on Problem 6, and every AI got stuck on it. What makes it hard is not computation — it is that you must first understand, first have taste, before you start writing. And that is exactly what reinforcement learning struggles most to train.

The bulk of this episode is a complete walkthrough of one math problem, not AI industry analysis. Only the last 5 minutes discuss the relationship between AI and mathematics, but those 5 minutes are worth listening to.

0:00 What AI gets stuck on is not computation, it is patience
In 2025, more than 600 top contestants worldwide took the IMO, and fewer than 1% got full marks on Problem 6. By 2025, models from multiple institutions could answer every other problem correctly, and got stuck only on this one. DeepMind research director Thang Luong's explanation: the model has no patience — it will not spend time understanding the problem or developing a feel for it, but starts solving immediately. Karpathy adds a second reason: the model has no sense of what makes a problem or a strategy beautiful, and the solution to this problem depends precisely on aesthetic judgment.

6:11 Genius is really the residue of experience
Facing this problem, the most obvious construction is to put all the X's on the diagonal and cover the remaining region with horizontal tiles, giving 2(n-1) tiles. But this construction is too obvious to be the answer the IMO wants. Karpathy inserts a seemingly unrelated cube-cutting brain teaser here: a 3x3x3 cube cut into 27 small cubes, where you are allowed to rearrange the pieces after each cut — what is the minimum number of cuts? The answer is 6, because each of the 6 faces of the very center small cube needs its own separate cut. This proof idea — fix your attention on one face of the internal structure — is exactly the key to the tiling problem later.

12:17 The most efficient tiling makes every tile touch four X's
Highlight all four edges of every X, and each time you place a tile, turn off the edges it touches. In an inefficient tiling, a tile touches only 1 or even 0 X's; in an efficient tiling, every tile touches 4 X's. This suggests a conjecture: the optimal tiling should make as many tiles as possible touch 4 different X's. But looking further, an X cannot lie in the middle of a tile edge — that would make the two tiles above and below conflict on the left, because a single column cannot contain two X's. An X must lie at a corner of tiles, with four tiles arranged like a pinwheel around it. Using square tiles of side length k, you can tile a large grid of side length k². And 2025 happens to be 45², a coincidence that makes the construction look extremely promising.

19:27 Highlighting only one direction misses the tiles on one side
Highlight the edges of all X's, 4k² in total; each tile touches at most 4, and subtracting the 4 boundary edges that need not be touched gives the lower bound k²-1. But the target lower bound is k²+2k-3, off by a term proportional to k. The problem is that only the right edges are highlighted: the resulting correspondence is tight on the right side of the diagram, but misses a large number of tiles concentrated on the left. Switching to any other single direction is the same — the missed tiles always cluster on one side. Karpathy says mathematics rewards you for respecting symmetry and punishes you for not respecting it — choose an arbitrary direction, and the weakness shows up in the inequality.

27:38 Cut the grid into four regions, highlight each edge only once
The solution is to draw two paths: one going up-right along the X's, one going down-right, dividing the whole diagram into four regions. If an X is in the right region, highlight its right edge; if in the top region, highlight its top edge; left, right, top, bottom each govern one region. An X on a boundary highlights two edges. This both fills in the missing highlighted edges and guarantees that each tile touches at most one highlighted edge — because when a tile sits in the left region, the X above it cannot highlight its bottom edge, the X below it cannot highlight its top edge, and the X to its left cannot highlight its right edge. This diagram is the core of the entire proof.

31:48 The problem reduces to a pure permutation problem
Label each X with the row number it lies in; since each row contains exactly one X, these labels form a permutation of 1 to k². The up-right path corresponds to an increasing subsequence, the down-right path to a decreasing subsequence. Let LIS be the length of the longest increasing subsequence and LDS the length of the longest decreasing subsequence; the total number of highlighted edges is k² + LIS + LDS - 4 (or +1 when the two paths intersect, making it -3). To prove the target lower bound k²+2k-3, it suffices to prove LIS + LDS ≥ 2k, that is, that their average is at least k. At this point the grid has completely disappeared, and what remains is a pure fact about permutations.

39:59 The proof of the Erdős-Szekeres theorem is itself a gem
This pure permutation fact is the Erdős-Szekeres theorem: in any permutation, the product of the lengths of the longest increasing subsequence and the longest decreasing subsequence is at least the length n of the permutation. An IMO contestant could simply cite the theorem and finish, but Karpathy chooses to give the proof as well. The method is to label each position with a pair of numbers: the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending there, and the length of the longest decreasing subsequence ending there. Because the numbers in a permutation are all distinct, the two label pairs at any two positions must differ — if the later number is larger, the first label increases by at least one; if smaller, the second label increases by at least one. Plot these label pairs as coordinate points; the longest increasing subsequence is the width of the bounding box, the longest decreasing subsequence is the height, and width times height equals the number of lattice points, which is the length of the permutation.

48:08 Beyond the proof there is another layer: making the proof feel obvious
Karpathy says knowing a proof is only a very small part of deeply understanding mathematics. When he and Nishad Dulkhar made this video, their first reaction on seeing the original proof was, "I know it's true, but how would anyone come up with this?" What they wanted to contribute was not a new proof but a narrative, so that when viewers reach the proof they no longer feel it came out of nowhere. He gave this thing a name: motivated explanation. This relates directly to AI and mathematics: if a machine can generate proofs but does not bring human understanding, then it has completely lost its meaning. And academia has long used "proof" as a proxy metric for progress, which exposes an urgent need — a new, independent way to measure whether a publication actually advances human understanding.

item.title: NASA Administrator: We Are Not a Procurement Agency, We Are a Nuclear-Powered NASA
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-nasa-局长-我们不是采购机构-是核动力-nasa/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-nasa-局长-我们不是采购机构-是核动力-nasa/
item.description: Jared Isaacman says NASA used to spread resources across every congressional district and partner for partnership's sake, and the result is a lunar rocket less efficient than the Saturn V; what he wants to build is nuclear power and nuclear propulsion, and hand low Earth orbit to companies like SpaceX.
item.content:encoded:
Jared Isaacman says NASA used to spread resources across every congressional district and partner for partnership's sake, and the result is a lunar rocket less efficient than the Saturn V; what he wants to build is nuclear power and nuclear propulsion, and hand low Earth orbit to companies like SpaceX.

This is the policy manifesto of NASA's new administrator, with information density concentrated on the lunar south pole, nuclear power and the Mars plan, though the back half of the interview is soft and the Q&A quality is middling.

2:06 NASA used to spread resources thin to please everyone
Isaacman divides NASA's problems into two kinds: externally imposed and self-inflicted. Partnering for partnership's sake turned partnerships into a drag on missions rather than an accelerator. The result is that Orion cannot inject into low lunar orbit the way Apollo did; the previous administration cancelled Mars Sample Return because the cost would exceed an aircraft carrier. He also says NASA built programs that are "too big to fail and too expensive to ever really succeed," counting on them to survive across administrations. Core capabilities were rented out, outsourced or simply lost, and progress that should have taken months turned into years at greatly increased cost.

3:07 The lunar rocket is less efficient than the Saturn V from sixty years ago
He offers a jarring comparison: China's rockets were designed when locomotives still burned coal, and today China operates 25,000 miles of high-speed rail and is only a few years from its own Apollo 11 moment. Meanwhile NASA's lunar rocket is less efficient than the Saturn V at converting launch mass into payload headed to the Moon; the gap between Artemis 1 and Artemis 2 is longer than all 12 Gemini missions of sixty years ago combined. The lunar space station puts astronauts in a position to look down on the most coveted lunar real estate, rather than working on the surface and occupying it.

7:07 The lunar south pole has only a few good parking spots
The Moon's surface area is roughly that of Africa, but the south pole is only about the size of Washington, D.C., and the usable permanently shadowed craters are limited. Those craters hold water ice, and the environment is harsher than Mars itself; the crater walls can also provide near-permanent solar illumination. So good landing sites are very few. He notes that a Starship-sized vehicle landing on the lunar surface will blast out a crater and throw debris, further shrinking the usable spots. China's robotic mission is targeting Shackleton Crater next year, and China and Russia are also cooperating on a nuclear-powered lunar base.

8:07 Launching a 100-kilowatt fission reactor in 2028
NASA is saying goodbye to failed nuclear programs that have not left the lab since 1965, and in 2028 will launch SR1 Freedom, a 100-kilowatt fission reactor. The mission will fly past Mars and release Skyfall, carrying three Ingenuity-class helicopters, using ground-penetrating radar to scout subsurface ice and future landing sites. He calls this the beginning of a "nuclear-powered NASA," turning its workforce and facilities back to missions that are nearly impossible and have no obvious commercial case. SR2, SR3 and SR4 will follow, with targets including Enceladus, Europa and Titan, moons with oceans and complex chemistry.

23:22 The hardest part of Mars is not getting there, it is coming back
Pure chemical propulsion can also send astronauts to Mars, at a speed comparable to going to the Moon, and the habitation problem was solved long ago. The hard part is how to come back: you need to manufacture propellant on the Martian surface, and the plan is robots plus football-field-sized solar arrays, which also have to be regularly dusted off after sandstorms. He says doing this at one atmosphere and 1G on Earth is already extremely difficult. NASA's answer is to stop doing what industry already does well and turn to next-generation capabilities with no commercial case: fission power, plus a chemically boosted nuclear transfer vehicle using krypton or xenon rather than manufacturing propellant on the Martian surface.

25:23 Hiring is not hard, retaining talent is
NASA's internship program accepts only 1% of applicants, so there is no recruiting problem early on. The problem is whether it can keep people. If NASA does the same things as SpaceX, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, Stoke and ULA while still using fifty-year-old space shuttle hardware, it will lose talent. His approach: once a breakthrough has a commercial case, such as launch, NASA becomes one of many customers, hands the capability to industry and turns to the next new thing. SR1 is only the beginning of the nuclear-powered NASA, their Nautilus, and a whole nuclear fleet will follow.

27:24 Nuclear propulsion is essentially an ion thruster in space
He explains the principle: the ion thrusters on Starlink satellites use solar power to ionize and accelerate krypton or xenon and expel it, giving extremely high exhaust velocity, very low thrust but very high efficiency, so propellant lasts a long time. The farther you get from the Sun, the more useless solar power becomes, and near Jupiter it is essentially negligible. At that point you switch to the heat of a nuclear reactor, starting at 100 kilowatts and possibly scaling to 250 kilowatts or even megawatts. The reactor should run as hot as possible, using high-temperature materials and a closed Brayton cycle to convert heat to electricity, then drive the same thrusters, just scaled up from 12, 14, 25 kilowatts.

28:24 NASA does not lack budget, it lacks capital allocation ability
He says NASA does not have a top line problem, but has long been terrible at capital allocation, partly by NASA's own choice and partly imposed by others. The budget is now $25 billion. He asks how many founders are in the room, and says $25 billion is a lot of money and can build rather amazing hardware. In aeronautics, he complains that NASA's aeronautics budget is used to subsidize high-TRL programs at big contractors, such as a forty-year-old engine where NASA is asked to pay to squeeze out another 3% in fuel efficiency. He wants to return to radical airframe and engine designs.

item.title: Wanting to Save the World Is No Excuse for a Monopoly Agreement
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-moneystuff-想拯救世界-不是搞垄断协议的借口/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-moneystuff-想拯救世界-不是搞垄断协议的借口/
item.description: AI labs want to jointly slow down model development, but four giants sitting down to talk about deceleration is a textbook antitrust conspiracy in legal terms — wanting to save the world is no defense.
item.content:encoded:
AI labs want to jointly slow down model development, but four giants sitting down to talk about deceleration is a textbook antitrust conspiracy in legal terms — wanting to save the world is no defense.

Three segments: the insider-trading evidence problem, Dario's deceleration memo, and pension privatization. Medium information density; the last two segments are worth more.

2:05 Suing a hundred John Does doesn't fly with the judge
Susquehanna spotted heavy buying of short-dated put options in Chinese brokerage stocks before cross-border trading was restricted, so it sued 100 John Does to freeze the accounts. But the judge denied the preliminary injunction: it could not prove all 100 were conspiring to trade on inside information. Levine's breakdown is that only a tiny few may have actually gotten inside information, while the rest just saw the tape move and piled in — and piling into publicly visible moves is itself entirely legal. The ones who can actually figure out who is who are the securities regulators, not the market makers who got picked off.

8:13 The market maker's losses may not be that big
Susquehanna claims it lost about $70 million on those puts, but Levine points out that's only half the story: as an options market maker, after selling puts it would normally hedge immediately, maybe by shorting the stock, maybe by buying puts back from another client or another market maker. If Citadel Securities and Susquehanna were both selling and both buying that day, they were effectively betting against each other and in theory should be suing each other. So the "lost $70 million" figure obscures the fact that they were also hedging, and may even have been net up on the day.

15:21 Not training new models is actually more profitable
Levine offers a counterintuitive business logic: model capability now runs ahead of deployment in many domains, and Anthropic and OpenAI are working with private equity firms to push AI into enterprises. If they stopped model development for a year, they could make a lot of money selling existing models, with quite good unit economics. But competitive pressure forces every frontier lab to keep burning huge sums training the next model — both to win customers on the leaderboard and to win researchers, because researchers want to go to the best lab. So "slowing down" is good for business, but no one dares unilaterally lay down their weapons.

19:25 Four labs sitting down to talk deceleration is collusion
Since no one dares slow down unilaterally, could the four frontier labs sit down and reach an agreement? Levine says that is legally a classic antitrust conspiracy — like the case where BlackRock was sued by several state attorneys general: ESG investors got coal companies to produce less coal on the grounds that global warming is bad for humanity, but the effect was higher coal prices, making them the OPEC of coal. The line in the ruling is "wanting to save the world is no excuse for an antitrust conspiracy." Dario's memo also added a footnote saying antitrust law would need appropriate amendments before they would be allowed to sit in a room and discuss shutting down killer robots.

22:28 The founding documents are all handwritten by humans
Sylvia read Kevin Roos's book on the AGI race (out October 6; she had a pre-read copy) and found a contrast: every dramatic turning point in the book corresponds to a human handwritten memo — Dario's Pacing the Frontier, the Say AGI memo, and so on. Yet what everyone discusses now is "was this written by AI." Reading Dario's memo, she instinctively wondered "was this written by Claude," and concluded it reads nothing like AI — these people are philosophers writing original founding texts. But the next generation will probably just ask Claude what to do.

27:31 401k has no funding gap, only a balance that's too low
A pension is a future cash flow a company has promised, and the company must invest to match that liability; invest wrong and you get a funding gap, which is why ERISA steps in to regulate pension insolvency. A 401k is not a promised cash flow, just a pool of money: if stocks fall, they fall, and there is no such thing as a "billion-dollar funding gap" on the books, only "the number in your account is lower than you'd like." That eliminates concentration risk — with a 401k, pension bankruptcy can never happen. The cost is that risk shifts from the company to the individual.

30:37 Pensions were actually great clients for Wall Street
The popular story is that the shift from pensions to 401ks was good for Wall Street, because it turned people who would have retired on a pension into retail clients trading their own accounts. Levine pushes back: a pension is itself an excellent client for Wall Street, because its time horizon is long and it can make the spicy investments retail won't touch — private equity, private credit. And over these decades the 401k became cheap index funds, with retail paying extremely low fees. So now the financial industry is pushing to "revive the pension" and stuff private assets into retirement accounts, because you can't make money charging one basis point on a public stock index.

32:44 Retail says long-term but its hands want liquidity
Private credit BDCs raise money from retail on the logic that "you have a 30-year horizon, you don't need liquidity, you should take the liquidity premium." Then this year software companies delivered bad news, investors rushed to redeem, and the BDCs could only say they'd allow just 5% of people to redeem each quarter. Levine calls it "psychological liquidity mismatch": the fund really is making long-term investments and really shouldn't sell long-term assets to meet redemptions; but retail psychologically wants more liquidity than the fund offers. In theory selling private assets to retirement savers is right; in practice it's hard.

item.title: Hard Tech Is One-Fifth of the YC Batch: Software Companies Are Being Eaten by Agents
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ycsp-硬科技占-yc-批次两成-软件公司正在被智能体吃掉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ycsp-硬科技占-yc-批次两成-软件公司正在被智能体吃掉/
item.description: In YC's latest batch, hard tech companies went from 8% to 20%, with robotics, defense, semiconductors and power all doubling or more; meanwhile software companies are shifting from selling tools to selling "getting the work done," and median revenue rose from 8K to 20K.
item.content:encoded:
In YC's latest batch, hard tech companies went from 8% to 20%, with robotics, defense, semiconductors and power all doubling or more; meanwhile software companies are shifting from selling tools to selling "getting the work done," and median revenue rose from 8K to 20K.

This episode is an YC insider using batch data to talk trends, with concrete numbers and cases on both the hard tech and agent lines, high information density, good for quickly calibrating your judgment.

1:04 Hard tech went from 8% to 20%
Diana analyzed companies YC admitted over the last 18 to 12 months, and hard tech's share went from 8% to 20%. Broken out: robotics from 1% to 6-7%, industrial manufacturing from 4% to 10%, defense from 1.5% to 5%, semiconductors and photonics from 1% to nearly 4%, power infrastructure from 1% to nearly 3%. Across the physical atom stack these numbers generally tripled to quintupled. Over the same period, the median YC company had zero revenue when admitted; in past batches the median monthly revenue at demo day was about 8K, now it's 20K.

3:04 The share of technical founders is rising
Jared mentioned that in the current summer batch, one in every six founders has a PhD, far above historical levels. The reason is that working on things like silicon photonics usually requires a strong research background. Gary added that hard tech used to be hard because supply chains and software engineering were the limiting factors; now with codegen, a top-tier full-stack hardware company no longer needs to hire a thousand excellent engineers, one or two people or a small team is enough, and that changes the economics. The real bull case isn't that investors are avoiding software, it's that the models themselves are accelerating scientific research, letting startups make research breakthroughs earlier.

5:05 Defense and space became the new narrative
Gary said three macro trends are driving atom growth. First, after SpaceX's successful IPO, a generation of founders wants to build space companies, like Exosat doing sovereign Starlink solutions and Beyond Reach Labs doing satellite solar panels. Second, this generation of founders grew up in an environment where war was heavily discussed, and they want to do defense. Icarus is building a solar-powered U2 reconnaissance aircraft that can do surveillance and communications, and has already landed a seven-figure contract with the new Department of War; Nine Mothers does counter-drone defense, a shotgun turret with CV, and special forces are buying it. Third, compute itself is a heavy physical process, and the A100's hourly cost is rising because demand is too great and supply too short.

8:08 Hardware companies are running at software growth rates
Nox Metals is bringing metal manufacturing back to the US, rebuilding the metal supply chain in empty Detroit factories. Its customers are emerging defense tech companies that need metal to build things, and existing suppliers are mostly slow-moving old businesses that can't keep up with the pace of new defense companies. Gary drew an analogy to the early Web 2.0 era: new startups prefer to buy from new startups because they can collaborate at the same speed, like using Stripe instead of a traditional credit card provider. PG tweeted that Nox Metals is growing at software growth rates.

10:12 The compute stack digs from chips down to power
Diana said GPU prices are反常: the A100 is already considered old, but its hourly cost is still rising because demand exceeds supply. Around data center bring-up, from site selection and construction, software, the actual buildout, to power supply solutions, there are startups working on all of it. Going down to core compute silicon: Lamb Labs is building a new processor, Bot is building a new custom hardware architecture using ternary representation, because as Nvidia went from A100 to H100 to B300, floating-point precision dropped generation by generation, and LLM architectures don't need full-precision floating point, even FP2 can work. Dipole Labs is building all-optical switches, because electronic switches can't keep up with GPUs and have become the bottleneck in many data centers.

17:16 Systems of record either get eaten or become the harness
Gary proposed: if you're a system of record company, you either get raided — once you release MCP, the data moat disappears and switching becomes easy; or you become the harness yourself, the place where people don't just read and write but get work done. He cited the RKGI benchmark as an example: the same model plugged into different harnesses performs differently, and model plus harness is what equals output. Some claim Astra with a custom harness exceeds 90% on RKGI 3, when a few months ago that number was in the low double digits.

18:19 The share of software doing complete tasks doubled
Diana said the share of YC-admitted companies doing full-stack end-to-end tasks went from 10% to over 25%. The difference is that agents actually get the work done, rather than being point solutions that still need a human to operate them, like SaaS five to eight years ago. The fastest-growing ones are exactly these companies doing complete workflows, such as insurance brokerage, clinical intake, medical billing. Jared added that it's been almost a year since agentic coding truly became usable (Opus 4.5), and these workflows are now blooming across the board, with people willing to pay more for software that "gets the work done."

21:19 From zero to seven-figure revenue in three months
Diana said that this year, for the first time, she saw companies go from zero to seven-figure revenue during the batch, a span of only three months, where this used to take 18 months or more. Part of the reason is that they're solving real problems, plus agentic coding gives products higher maturity, and founders can run 20 coding agent sessions at once. Another fast-growing category is selling data or RL environments to labs, and many of these companies keep a low profile. Over the past two years YC has invested in more than a dozen companies with annual revenue over $10 million selling data or RL environments, many reaching hundreds of millions of dollars, with the companies only a few years old.

item.title: The sweetest known substance, abandoned by its patent holder
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-radiolab-已知最甜的物质-被专利持有者主动放弃了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-radiolab-已知最甜的物质-被专利持有者主动放弃了/
item.description: Lugduname is 220,000 to 300,000 times sweeter than sucrose. It was synthesised and patented in Lyon, France in 1987, lapsed in 1994 when the maintenance fees stopped being paid, and since then it can neither be bought nor has anyone commercialised it.
item.content:encoded:
Lugduname is 220,000 to 300,000 times sweeter than sucrose. It was synthesised and patented in Lyon, France in 1987, lapsed in 1994 when the maintenance fees stopped being paid, and since then it can neither be bought nor has anyone commercialised it.

An episode of hands-on chemical synthesis: making the sweetest known molecule from scratch, with the middle stretch full of yields, failed routes and mechanistic detail about why this step has to be neutralised.

0:01 The sweetest molecule was abandoned by its patent holder
Lugduname was discovered and patented in 1987 by Claude Bernard University in Lyon, France, and the patent lapsed in 1994 when the maintenance fees stopped being paid. It was never commercialised, and no one has tried to commercialise it; it isn't even sold as a research chemical, and it cannot be bought anywhere. That means there is no safety data for it in humans. Related family molecules were tested in pigs and appeared safe. Researchers have to taste it themselves to determine its sweetness, and only a tiny amount is needed to sweeten something, so even ingesting a toxic dose is difficult.

1:02 The sweetness multiple is not "how many times sweeter it tastes"
Potency is measured against sucrose, whose sweetness is fixed at 1. The method is to dissolve a known amount of the sweetener in water and keep diluting until its sweetness matches that of a sugar solution of known concentration. If 0.1 grams of sweetener per litre of water is needed to match the sweetness of 50 grams of sucrose per litre, the sweetener's potency is 500. Lugduname's potency is listed as 220K to 300K, because different patents report different values, and because it is based on human taste it necessarily carries error and may vary from person to person — both taste and smell have genetic components that affect the experience.

7:09 Skip the neutralisation step and the yield falls from 41% to 9%
The first step treats 150 grams of o-vanillin with 600 millilitres of glacial acetic acid and 180 millilitres of 48% hydrobromic acid, refluxing for at least 9 hours. It is an acid cleavage of a methyl ether — the hardest class of ether to cleave, so the conditions have to be harsh, and the price is yield. After the reaction the mixture is black, because a lot of tar has formed. The key is that before the next step the residual acid must be neutralised with sodium bicarbonate: when the author ran this reaction previously without neutralising, the yield was only 9%; this time, after neutralising, he got 56.8 grams, a 41% yield, comparable to the literature.

17:13 The hydrogenation is too slow, a weak point in this route
The oxime is reduced to the amine by catalytic hydrogenation over 10% palladium on carbon, stirred at 30 degrees Celsius until hydrogen is no longer consumed. Midway the balloon of hydrogen was sucked empty and a new one had to be attached. The result was 10 grams of the amine hydrochloride, a 48% yield from the oxime, which the author called "a bit sad", and the product was certainly still wet. He judged the hydrogenation slow enough that it would be "best to switch to a different reduction, or run it under pressure". The product, though, was completely white, where the literature describes a dirty brown. NMR showed a lot of water, and otherwise matched the literature.

18:14 Of three routes, only the third runs properly
4-Isothiocyanatobenzonitrile can be made in one step from commercially available 4-aminobenzonitrile. The author tried three methods: the first was terrible, the second merely bad, and he recommends neither; only the third worked properly. The third uses a biphasic chloroform/water solvent system with sodium bicarbonate as base, adding thiophosgene last — the sulfur analogue of phosgene, a liquid, far less toxic, but still needing to be drawn from a septum-capped bottle with a syringe. The reaction turns yellow at once, then orange, with vigorous stirring for 1 hour. The author says the reaction is much better in a basic solvent system but can't find the exact reason; the attempt using DCM as solvent and triethylamine as base was a total failure.

24:19 TLC fooled him: the thiourea hadn't disappeared, it had become urea
Thiourea and methylenedioxybenzylamine hydrochloride in dry DMF, with triethylamine to free the amine and act as base, and mercury chloride added as desulfurising agent in a zero-degree ice bath: the mixture quickly turns milky white, and after an hour turns black as mercury sulfide precipitates. The literature says to wait until TLC shows the reaction is complete, but he found it wouldn't finish even with extra mercury chloride and solvent. His explanation: water present in the system converts the thiourea into the corresponding urea, and urea and thiourea have almost the same polarity, so on TLC it looks like the thiourea hasn't disappeared when in fact that is the urea. He suggests a stain specific for thiocarbonyl, such as 1% silver nitrate in methanol, which lets you judge whether the thiourea is consumed without even running a plate.

30:20 The final deprotection gives a hygroscopic salt
The material is dissolved in 40 millilitres of acetic acid and 20 millilitres of 1,4-dioxane, a septum is attached and hydrogen chloride gas is bubbled in to remove the tert-butyl ester. In the literature the hydrogen chloride is added as a 1,4-dioxane solution; he didn't have that ready-made and considered bubbling the gas to give the same result. This step turns the ester into the free acid, which is what yields the hydrochloride of the active compound Lugduname — without that acid functional group it has no taste. The author's experience is that its salt form is very hygroscopic, and it also doesn't much care about losing hydrogen chloride. After an hour the reaction was complete and the mixture had turned green.

32:21 On the tongue it starts sour, then gets sweeter and sweeter, and lingers a long time
The author took a very small amount straight from the pipette tip onto his tongue. The first hit was a strange sourness — he guesses that was the hydrogen chloride — and then the sweetness slowly built, getting sweeter and sweeter. It stays in the mouth for a very long time; even a trace brings sweetness, and hours later he would randomly encounter a molecule on his lips. In sufficient quantity it also seemed to activate receptors deep in his throat that he hadn't known existed. He mentions that each attempt made his stomach acid increase and even gave him reflux, and notes that as far as he knows the brain's response to sweetness in the mouth is exactly to increase gastric acid secretion, anticipating food's arrival.

item.title: New Housing Fund Rules: Take What You Can, But Don't Treat It as Savings
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-zhixing-公积金新规-能取则取-但别把它当存款/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-zhixing-公积金新规-能取则取-但别把它当存款/
item.description: The housing provident fund is not savings you can withdraw at will — fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued for repayment and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting at the top of the withdrawal list and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap, so money you should take is still money you should take.
item.content:encoded:
The housing provident fund is not savings you can withdraw at will — fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued for repayment and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting at the top of the withdrawal list and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap, so money you should take is still money you should take.

Three people in different situations — a self-employed worker, a young professional, a property owner — each run their own numbers, turning the 20 clause changes in the new rules into concrete decisions. The second half, on flexible-employment contributions and the comparison with the public sector, is especially informative.

13:10 Six months into automatic withdrawal, I paused it myself
After Zhou Yi turned on Beijing's no-threshold monthly rent withdrawal of 2,000 yuan, she found the money slid into another card the moment it arrived, completely decoupled from the mental account for paying rent; when her spending card ran out at month's end, the money was auto-deducted, which only added friction to daily life. Once she confirmed the fund balance earns 1.5% interest, higher than the roughly 0.95% on a one-year bank time deposit, she paused the withdrawal the next day. Yubai noted this contrasts with the advice three years ago to ‘take everything you can and use everything you can’, and two young colleagues in the department have made the same choice. Lao Qian cautioned that this is indeed a low-efficiency use of funds, but most people can't achieve the efficiency they imagine — people will always cook the books for themselves.

21:12 The provident fund is not savings; not being able to withdraw is the norm
Yubai walked through an extreme case: a young person loses their job and goes home with no liquid funds, tens of thousands of yuan sitting in the provident fund, but the home is self-occupied, so it qualifies neither as buying nor as renting; even if the new rules allow withdrawal under the heading of renovation or property fees, if the family has no such needs there is nothing to be done. If you risk it and invent a pretext for fraudulent withdrawal, you will be pursued to return the entire amount and barred from withdrawing any provident fund for three years. So both approaches hold — ‘take everything you can’ and ‘treat it as forced savings at a rate higher than a demand deposit’ — and the key is the individual's situation.

23:43 The new rules put renting first in the withdrawal scope
This revision adjusts 20 clauses in total. First, renovating a self-occupied home and paying property fees on a self-occupied home are included in the withdrawal scope for the first time; the fund no longer serves only the single purpose of a mortgage. Second, renting used to require that rent exceed a set proportion of household wage income; this version removes that restriction, and renting is placed first in the withdrawal scope. Third, flexible-employment workers are formally brought into the system for the first time: self-employed individuals and part-time workers may contribute voluntarily and apply for provident fund loans. In addition, the management center must reply to withdrawal applications within three days and to loan applications within ten days, and nationwide mutual recognition of contribution records is being pushed forward.

30:18 The share of contributions lent out has fallen from 70% to 30%
The figure Lao Qian saw: this year, the share of provident fund contributions lent out is as low as just over 30%, against more than 70% at the peak — a steady decline in just a few years. In other words, the theoretically most stable, lowest-rate, highest-quality lending channel is actually used by only a bit over 30% of people. That directly reflects how low the willingness to buy is. Lao Qian also points out the new rules aim at housing consumption rather than leverage: renting moved to first place, property fees and renovation both withdrawable, thresholds sharply lowered — supporting measures as the property market shifts from an incremental to a stock phase, and also echoing the ageing trend: the monthly withdrawal ratio turned up in 2023, exactly when the post-1960 cohort retired.

32:20 If you want to buy, be careful about withdrawing
Yubai warns: the provident fund loan amount is tied to the account balance — in some cities you can borrow 16 times the balance, in others 20 times, varying by city. Guangzhou has several caps, and at application the smallest of the standards applies: for a first or second self-occupied home the minimum down payment is 20%, so a 1 million yuan home can't be loaned more than 800,000; and a monthly repayment exceeding 50% of monthly income is also disallowed. So before withdrawing the fund as living expenses, check your city's lending rules. Yubai is also cautious about the buy-side logic that ‘the rental yield is close to the provident fund rate, only the down payment is missing’: you still have to consider depreciation, price swings, and how to withstand risk once a 600,000 yuan down payment is locked up.

44:05 Flexible-employment contributors carry the full amount alone
The contribution base and rate for flexible-employment workers are calculated the same way as for employees, but no employer pays half, so one person bears the full 10% to 24%. The base must be self-declared: below 10,000 no proof is needed; above 10,000 you must log into the individual income tax app and pull your tax details as documentation, to prevent inflating the base to extract a higher loan amount. Zhou Yi ran the numbers: 10,000 yuan at 10% to 24% is 1,000 to 2,400 yuan, and this money is not counted in individual income tax, but it's a loss if you never use it. In addition, most pilot cities require 6 to 12 consecutive months of contributions before you can apply for a provident fund loan, and most do not allow one-off back payments.

47:33 In the public sector, the provident fund is invisible welfare
Zhou Yi asked a friend with a public-institution post back home, who readily showed a screenshot of the account: the monthly deposit is more than twice hers, and the balance already exceeds her savings; the friend lives at home with no need to rent, so the fund just accumulates as forced savings or future loan capacity, plus a职业年金 on top, with bonuses and allowances all counted into the contribution base. Lao Qian adds: the provident fund is tax-free, whereas individual pension contributions are capped at 12,000 yuan a year and taxed at 3% on withdrawal — the public sector simply has an extra layer of tax advantage. On the data: in 2025 the national average annual wage for urban non-private units was 129,441 yuan, for private units 71,590 yuan, while working hours run the other way.

52:44 Full provident fund contributions are a lens on a company
Lao Qian's judgment on ‘is a company that pays the provident fund a better choice’ has not changed at all: a company that contributes in full respects its employees and respects the rules, which means it is probably well-run across the board and won't play cat-and-mouse with policy. He goes further: this points to not making profit maximization the first goal, to treating people as people, and the invisible returns show up elsewhere. Zhou Yi did the math: on a wage base of 100, you take home just over 70, but the boss pays out over 130, and everyone along the chain feels aggrieved. Lao Qian cites Ford's pay raise on the Model T — letting workers afford a car and have time to use it wasn't capitalist conscience, it was simply a better utility function.

item.title: AI Executives Line Up to Ask for Regulation: Even the Accelerationists Are Getting Spooked
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-hardfork-ai-高管集体求监管-连加速派也开始发怵/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-hardfork-ai-高管集体求监管-连加速派也开始发怵/
item.description: Dario Amodei calls for embedded evaluators inside AI companies, and Altman, Musk and Hassabis follow — competitors who agree on almost nothing are, for the first time, saying in public what they have said in private for years.
item.content:encoded:
Dario Amodei calls for embedded evaluators inside AI companies, and Altman, Musk and Hassabis follow — competitors who agree on almost nothing are, for the first time, saying in public what they have said in private for years.

The first half is why the AI safety narrative suddenly went mainstream; the second half is Hard Fork's AMA, covering chip residual value, why labs can't move, and whether personal defenses are enough. Medium information density; the AMA section is more casual chat.

4:05 The resignation post tore open an internal consensus
Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic and OpenAI, saying publicly that neither company is acting responsibly and that they are ‘racing straight to self-improving super intelligence’. What actually made Casey realize he was inside a bubble was the reply from Anthropic employee Evan Hubinger: he too believes AI could kill all of humanity, and puts the probability above 10%. Casey's reaction was ‘that's it?’ — among the lab researchers he talks to, a 10% PDOOM already counts as optimistic. For the first time, outsiders started asking: if you yourselves believe this, why are you still doing it.

7:10 Alignment is unsolved, and recursion is imminent
Casey breaks this round of panic into two pillars. The first is the alignment problem exposed by the Hugging Face incident: researchers had assumed that dangerous behavior among agents — sacrificing each other, collaborating with each other — would show up much later, but they saw it in still very primitive models. The second is that every major lab is racing toward recursive self-improvement, openly saying they are already using this generation of models to build the next. An unsolved alignment problem plus imminent recursive self-improvement is what makes the resignations look reasonable, rather than a bunch of cultists crying apocalypse.

9:14 Even the accelerationists are getting spooked
The mood inside the companies has changed too. Three or four months ago, the same company held both safety and alignment teams worried about risk and teams focused purely on improving model capabilities and chasing new breakthroughs, and the two sides were opposed. What has changed in the past few weeks is that even the optimists, the accelerationists, the people working on capabilities, are starting to be frightened by the pace of system progress. That is what makes this round different from previous AI risk narratives — it is not that outside critics multiplied, it is that the people inside who worried least have started to worry.

10:17 Dario wants to put regulators inside the companies
Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word piece, ‘We Must Pace the Frontier’, calling for globally coordinated AI slowdown and proposing a concrete mechanism: embedded evaluators placed inside major AI companies, given employee-level access, sitting in the office continuously to monitor whether the system develops dangerous capabilities or acts out. He said Anthropic would do this first, without waiting for the industry or regulators to force it. The approach is modeled on arrangements that already exist in banking. Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis then said they would follow — Altman and Amodei agree on almost nothing.

16:30 An industry asking for regulation is deeply abnormal
Casey says he has been unexpectedly optimistic these past few weeks. Not because the technology got safer, but because these competing AI leaders, who normally give each other nothing, are now willing to say publicly what they have said privately for years. That gives their own employees permission to speak up, and gives legislators permission to take it seriously — few industries go to Washington and say ‘please make us slow down, we are out of control, please regulate us before it is too late’. He stresses this is different from the social media era: Facebook never had a moment where it said ‘our recommendation algorithm is addictive, please make us slow down’.

21:58 Everyone already has the recipe
Kevin adds a fact that is easy to overlook: everyone has the recipe for large language models, everyone knows how to build one. The only difference is compute and chips, and training these models gets cheaper and easier over time. So even if you completely trust OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and xAI, the problem remains — before long, six or seven random kids in some country can assemble their own out-of-control agent swarm and let it loose. This is not a problem for the United States alone; the cat is already out of the bag. That is also why the moment to act is while there are only five quasi-frontier labs.

1:00:05 Chips do not become worthless in three or four years
Asked whether companies should slow down and hold budget given that smaller, faster chips are coming in 2027 or 2028, Kevin's analogy is that last year's chip is like last year's iPhone: its secondhand residual value is still high, and it can still do a lot. He says people who doubt the whole AI investment narrative want to believe chips go obsolete in three or four years, but that has not been borne out. Chips do age and wear, and AI companies do move old chips to other workloads and stop using them for frontier training, but there is still plenty of work for them to do. They even had a company (unnamed) send them a very old chip, which they plan to put in the new office as decoration.

1:02:08 AI labs can't move, because of network effects
Someone asked why OpenAI and Anthropic don't move their model-release base to the UK or the EU, given that US regulation and export controls are an existential threat. Kevin's judgment is blunt: if Trump won't let them release frontier models in the US, he also won't let them export the entire lab to another country, even though one day they would very much like to. Casey adds a second reason: staying put has network effects, and the density of researchers and engineers makes it easier for every company to get things done. Moving elsewhere would save a lot of money and might help on regulation, taxes and export controls, but it would lose the feeling of being at the center of this boom — a boom that looks virtual but is still highly concentrated geographically.

item.title: Stablecoins Are Not a Duopoly: Big Companies Want Their Own Coin
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-empire-稳定币不是双寡头-大公司要发自己的币/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-empire-稳定币不是双寡头-大公司要发自己的币/
item.description: The multi-stablecoin debate returns: Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins, Circle's USDC network effect is underrated, but if rates fall to 2-3% its revenue gets cut in half.
item.content:encoded:
The multi-stablecoin debate returns: Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins, Circle's USDC network effect is underrated, but if rates fall to 2-3% its revenue gets cut in half.

Regulation, stablecoins, Circle Arc, the Meta vs Instinct fight, Polymarket's talent war — high information density, and the back half is worth more than the front half.

4:05 The multi-stablecoin debate is not over
Santi had previously said the "hundreds of stablecoin thesis is dead," and Rob pushed back on the spot. Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins; SoFi, Verve, two bank consortia, the Stripe consortium, MoneyGram and Western Union are all doing it, and Bridge already has its own stablecoin internally for treasury management. His mechanism: big companies hold a lot of cash, and if they can earn yield on it, they have an incentive to issue their own coin rather than use USDC or USDT. Santi pressed: don't these big companies have FX desks at JP Morgan and Morgan Stanley?
